items.abstract_text: Compute-in-memory (CiM) offers a promising solution to the hardware challenges faced in artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT), particularly in tackling the “memory wall” problem. By leveraging non-volatile memory (NVM) devices arranged in a crossbar structure, CiM efficiently accelerates multiply-accumulate (MAC) computations, which are essential for neural networks and various AI models. Emerging NVM, i.e., Ferroelectric FET (FeFET), is a particularly appealing choice for constructing ultra-low-power CiM arrays due to its CMOS compatibility, voltage-driven write/read mechanisms and high I ON /I OFF ratio. Operating FeFETs in the subthreshold region, i.e., subthreshold-FeFETs, further reduces power, but introduces vulnerability to temperature drift, leading to potential accuracy degradation. In this article, we present subthreshold-FeFET based temperature-resilient 2T-1FeFET and 2FeFET-1T CiM cell designs that address the temperature vulnerability. These two cells leverage feedback mechanisms to minimize the output current fluctuations caused by temperature drift. We further propose GTRCiM, a novel generic temperature-resilient CiM design that accommodates both our proposed CiM cells and other typical FeFET based cells while maintaining ultra-low-power consumption with subthreshold-FeFETs. By incorporating an additional column of the CiM array as a reference, and leveraging the temperature-resilient cell design, GTRCiM compensates for the effects of temperature drift, as temperature affects both arrays uniformly. We integrate the proposed GTRCiM array with typical 1FeFET-1R, and our proposed 2T-1FeFET, 2FeFET-1T cells and validate that GTRCiM enhances the temperature resilience with our proposed cells and even the temperature vulnerable 1FeFET-1R cell. Benchmarking results at system level using the NeuroSim framework show that our proposed GTRCiM array integrated with subthreshold-FeFET based 1FeFET-1R cells achieves 28.09 TOPS/W energy efficiency, surpassing existing CiM designs while maintaining sufficient temperature resilience.

items.abstract_text: Accurate and fast timing prediction at early design stages is crucial for achieving timing closure in very-large-scale integration (VLSI) design. Machine learning (ML) based approaches have been widely adopted for timing prediction to pursue both accuracy and speed. Unfortunately, these approaches fail to fully exploit the layout features, which can significantly impact the timing metrics, thus leading to great accuracy degradation. In this article, we propose LE-Timing, an end-to-end layout-aware timing prediction approach that can achieve better accuracy by leveraging important layout information. The key insight is that crucial information about coupling capacitance between routing wires can significantly impact timing metrics, and fully exploiting this layout information in the timing prediction model can substantially improve its accuracy. However, efficiently leveraging layout features while maintaining accuracy poses three key challenges: node-level layout-graph integration, domain experience utilization and training efficiency. To address these, we further propose three key technologies specially designed for LE-Timing correspondingly, including a layout-encoding net model, an explainable cell model, and an explicit-message-passing scheme. Experimental results on 16 open-source designs with an advanced 7-nm technology node demonstrate that LE-Timing achieves R 2 score 0.94 for arrival time prediction and lower error accumulation compared to the baselines.

items.abstract_text: Predicting electromigration (EM) stress is a critical reliability challenge in power delivery networks. Existing semi-analytical Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) models neglect the Markovian sequential dependencies of EM diffusion and suffer from severe scalability issues due to global topological evaluations. To address these architectural and computational bottlenecks, this article proposes a dynamic spatiotemporal stress forecasting framework. Specifically, a physics-aligned Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is constructed to directly model the Markovian sequential evolution of EM stress. This is integrated with a tensor mapping-based dynamic local subgraph extraction strategy, effectively isolating spatial complexity from the global interconnect scale. At the numerical integration level, we develop a physics-driven adaptive hybrid convolution algorithm. Regulated by a stress relaxation time constant, this algorithm dynamically invokes discrete convolution during the early acceleration phase to strictly preserve the abrupt variations of the auxiliary function used for stress computation, and seamlessly switches to Gauss-Legendre quadrature during stable periods to maximize precision while eliminating smoothing artifacts. Furthermore, a simulation-time-based optimization strategy is incorporated to mitigate the prediction error gap between early and late simulation stages. Experimental results validate the efficiency of the proposed framework. Compared with the MLP baseline, our model achieves up to a 93.2% reduction in relative error and a 117.79× computational speedup. Against the Finite Element Method (FEM), it delivers up to 1335.6× acceleration while maintaining engineering-grade accuracy.

items.title: Power Switch Network Optimization Using Machine Learning for Inrush Current and Wakeup Latency Prediction
items.journal: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.venue_name: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.summary: Today’s large-scale designs leverage power gating to achieve low power consumption, which necessitates the design of an efficient power switch network that accounts for both inrush current and wakeup latency. Optimizing this power switch network involves striking a balance between minimizing inrush current and reducing wakeup latency. However, analyzing inrush and wakeup latency for a given network is computationally expensive, particularly for complex systems, making optimization frameworks that rely on analysis engines prohibitively slow. To address this challenge, we frame the analysis of inrush and wakeup latency as a regression problem and train machine-learning (ML) models to predict these metrics. The ML model achieves mean errors of less than 10% for inrush current prediction and for wakeup latency prediction, while providing a speedup of over 50× compared to SPICE. By leveraging an ML model, we efficiently explore the design space and identify optimized power switch network patterns that minimize both wakeup latency and inrush current.

items.abstract_text: With the continuous advancement of semiconductor technology, the explosive increase in the number of corners to be covered during chip design has imposed severe challenges on timing analysis resource and time cost. Recent studies on machine learning-based cross-corner timing prediction have emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating multi-corner timing analysis. Those existing approaches predominantly rely on precomputed multi-corner timing analysis results or process technology parameters for model training, but suffer from limited industrial adoption due to the large number of training corners, the complex pre-training flow, and the opaque nature of the black-box architecture. In case of this, we propose an XGBoost-based cross-corner timing analysis framework that requires only a single-corner static timing analysis report as input to achieve high-precision timing prediction with an average mean absolute error of approximately 1.604 ps across corners. The proposed methodology has been validated through commercial projects based on different deep nanometer process nodes (7 nm and below), demonstrating robust performance stability. In the task of critical path identification and optimization, this proposed method achieves near-100% coverage with acceptable increase in additional STA overhead. Furthermore, we employ SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis to interpret the XGBoost model, quantifying key contributors to cross-corner timing variations. This not only enhances the explainability of the black-box model but also provides insights for design optimization and robustness improvement.

items.title: Multi-Scale Feature Refinement Network for Lithography Hotspot Detection
items.journal: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.venue_name: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.summary: As semiconductor manufacturing advances toward smaller process nodes and more complex layouts, lithography hotspot detection faces increasing challenges. Traditional methods often struggle to capture subtle geometric variations in complex layouts, resulting in low recall and high False Alarm Rate (FA). To address this problem, we propose a Multi-Scale Feature Refinement Network (MSFRN). The key innovation lies in a collaborative “Extraction–Refinement–Decision” framework specifically designed for Hard-To-Classify samples: the Multi-Scale Feature Extraction module comprehensively captures rich information ranging from local geometric details to global layout context; the Feature Refinement Network enhances responses to critical geometric features through a lightweight gating mechanism; and finally, ConvNeXt serves as the decision module, integrating and classifying the refined features for final hotspot prediction. Experimental results show that on the most challenging ICCAD 2019-2 benchmark, MSFRN improves recall by up to 11.3%, with the FA varying from a 0.2% increase to a 5.8% reduction, demonstrating superior detection capability.

items.abstract_text: The emerging graphene interconnect technology is expected to be a promising alternative to traditional interconnect technologies due to its superior conductivity. Because of the dominant impact of global routing on the overall performance of a widely used application, the Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), this work investigates the potential advantage of using graphene-based interconnects to replace conventional copper (Cu) for global routing. Furthermore, a scalability analysis is performed, and the effects of technology node scaling from 7 nm to 1.5 nm are evaluated using lateral gate-all-around field-effect transistors (LGAAFETs) within the proposed system-technology co-design (STCO) framework. Key material-level parameters, including the mean free path (MFP), contact resistance, and the number of graphene layers, are systematically analyzed. Benchmark simulations demonstrate that a 32% improvement in the energy-delay product (EDP) is achieved with graphene-based interconnects compared to Cu counterparts at the 7 nm technology node, and an additional 46% reduction is observed at the 1.5 nm technology node. It is important to note that this work is an exploratory STCO study incorporating cross-layer design considerations, with a focus on long-term trends rather than short-term manufacturability.

items.title: ODCGate: Leveraging Observability Don’t Care Conditions for Enhanced Power Efficiency in Clock Gating
items.journal: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.venue_name: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.summary: Clock gating reduces dynamic power by integrating activation functions and integrated clock gating (ICG) cells into the clock path, selectively disabling the clock signal to register when unnecessary. While conventional activation function extraction methods rely on manual design or register-transfer level analysis, a gate-level alternative exists: deriving activation functions through the extraction of observability don’t care (ODC) conditions from the underlying netlist. This article presents ODCGate , a framework designed to automatically detect ODC conditions as the activation functions and safely block clock transitions for unused registers, thereby further reducing dynamic power consumption during clock gating. The computation begins with cut boundary enumeration and simulation. To further minimize additional PPA overhead, we apply hybrid simplification techniques to the extracted logic, and enable sharing among registers through clustering. Experimental results show that, beyond the clock gating optimization of a commercial logic synthesis tool, our method achieves an average 33.46% additional reduction in dynamic power, with minimal impact on other PPA metrics.

items.title: SEC-CiM+: Selective and Reconfigurable Error Compensation for ReRAM-based Compute-in-Memory
items.journal: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.venue_name: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.summary: ReRAM-based Compute-in-Memory (CiM) architectures provide a promising solution for accelerating Deep Neural Network (DNN) inference in edge computing environments. However, these architectures are susceptible to stuck-at faults (SAFs), including stuck-at intermediate states, which degrade inference accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a reconfigurable error compensation (EC) mechanism that selectively mitigates errors while operating under memory constraints. By leveraging an indexed storage format, our approach efficiently compensates for errors without excessive overhead. We develop a theoretical framework to determine the minimum number of critical columns requiring compensation and analyze how EC transitions between three modes of operation across different models. The EC mechanism requires only 0.3874 mW of additional power for single operational-unit correction and introduces negligible latency overhead, while sustaining near-baseline accuracy for DenseNet121, VGG16, ResNet18, and SwinT under high fault densities (5–10%). Moreover, the overall energy overhead remains below 6% for ResNet18 and VGG16, and below 10% for DenseNet121.

items.abstract_text: Very Long Instruction Word (VLIW) architectures deliver compelling performance-energy-cost advantages for automotive, AI, and high-performance computing. However, a persistent performance-productivity gap limits broader adoption: manual assembly optimization achieves superior performance but requires substantial expertise, while automated compilation underperforms. Existing assembly-level optimization tools commit to single scheduling strategies, unable to adapt to diverse program patterns. This article presents LASM, the first symbolic assembly framework enabling competitive multi-strategy orchestration for complete VLIW programs. Rather than committing to a single algorithm, multiple scheduling strategies simultaneously optimize identical code regions, with the framework automatically selecting the top solution through feasibility-driven ranking. LASM features standardized extension interfaces enabling plugin-style strategy integration and unified scheduling primitives eliminating algorithmic redundancy. We contribute two novel strategies: Longevity-Aware Expanded Modulo Scheduling (LAEMS) with dependency relaxation, proactive reordering, and parallel expansion search, and Front-Back Block Fusion (FBBF) for cross-boundary scheduling. Evaluation on 13 benchmarks across two production VLIW-SIMD processors demonstrates LASM achieves 103.6% and 101.6% of expert assembly performance while reducing manual code by 72.6%. A full YOLOv5 deployment validates production applicability at 95.9% of expert performance. Code is available at https://github.com/urays/lasm.

items.abstract_text: In PCB design, engineers often rely on datasheets to obtain crucial chip information, a process that is both time-consuming and labor-intensive. To streamline this workflow, we present PCB-QA, a task-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based question-answering system that automatically addresses text-centric chip-related queries using the latest datasheets. Rather than aiming to replace broader commercial AI-assisted EDA platforms, this work focuses on a narrower and reproducible research problem: grounded datasheet question answering over a maintained corpus. While existing RAG technologies have made significant progress in document-based question answering, several challenges remain, primarily due to the erroneous segmentation of documents, the retrieval of inaccurate references, and under-specified user queries. To improve the accuracy of PCB-QA’s responses, our framework incorporates three key components. First, we propose a datasheet segmentation model that is specifically trained to divide the corpus into semantically coherent chunks. Second, we integrate a correlation estimation module to better assess the relevance of retrieved references and reduce the influence of distractors. Finally, recognizing that user inputs may lack critical details, we employ a query-rationalization mechanism to facilitate further reasoning and refine the query for under-specified technical and application-related questions. These task-specific customizations improve retrieval quality and support more accurate grounded answers for datasheet-centric QA. Experimental results on our customized ChipQuestion benchmark demonstrate that PCB-QA achieves consistent improvements over representative RAG baselines on text-grounded datasheet QA. We also clarify the current scope of PCB-QA: the present implementation is primarily text-centric and does not yet fully address image-only figures, waveform plots, complex visual tables, or other visuallygrounded datasheet content.

items.abstract_text: The performance enhancements of coarse-grain reconfigurable cryptographic arrays (CGRCAs) through technology upgrades and increasing chip size are approaching limits. Enhancing parallel processing capabilities can relieve the computational burden on CGRCA in high-density computing scenarios. Specifically, a novel parallel processing approach is introduced in this article, named virtual heterogeneous multi-core pipelining (VHMP). VHMP supports virtual heterogeneous multi-core and intra-core multitask pipelining. Informed by hardware virtualization principles and analysis of CGRCA architectures, VHMP constructs virtual computing cores (VCCs) on CGRCA using multi-launch pipelines and implements multitask interleave pipelines within each VCC, enabling parallel processing at pipeline, task, and instruction levels. Furthermore, a hierarchical control mechanism is embedded within VHMP, integrating virtual computing path level and task-level management. This control mechanism allows diverse cryptographic algorithms to run concurrently without being bound to specific types or modes. Finally, applying VHMP to a 32 × 4 CGRCA, 32 heterogeneous VCCs are instantiated, with each core handling up to 16 interleaved tasks. Compared to treating CGRCA as a homogeneous multi-core processor, the VHMP approach achieves an average acceleration of 4.33 × (up to 6.34 ×) with quadrupled instruction execution capability. Additionally, the control mechanism reduces context volume to 18.7% and boosts configuration speed by 3 ×. Compared with related architectures, VHMP improves CGRCA throughput by an average of 5.3 ×.

items.abstract_text: Understanding the functionality of Boolean networks is crucial for processes such as functional equivalence checking, logic synthesis, and malicious logic identification. With the proliferation of deep learning in electronic design automation (EDA), graph neural networks (GNNs) are widely used to embed and-inverter graphs (AIGs)—a standard form of Boolean networks—into vectorized representations. A key challenge in applying GNNs for Boolean representation is that although GNNs can effectively encapsulate the structural properties of AIGs, they struggle to efficiently capture Boolean logic functionality. In this work, we focus on breaking this bottleneck by enhancing the functional representation capability of GNNs, proposing PolarGate, an efficient solution that not only aligns message passing with AIG logical functionality but also effectively integrates global information. Leveraging the intrinsic ambipolar states (0 and 1) of AIG nodes, PolarGate maps gate behavior into an ambipolar state space, customizes differentiable logical operators, and designs a functionality-aware message passing strategy. To further capture global circuit information, PolarGate integrates a structure-aware preprocessing module and a global linear attention module, transcending the locality constraint of message passing. Experimental results on two functionality-related basic tasks (signal probability prediction and truth-table distance prediction) and a downstream task (logic equivalence prediction) show that PolarGate outperform state-of-the-art GNN-based methods.

items.title: Faster Random Walk-based Capacitance Extraction with Generalized Antithetic Sampling
items.journal: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.venue_name: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.summary: Floating random walk-based capacitance extraction has emerged in recent years as a tried and true approach for extracting parasitic capacitance in very large scale integrated circuits. Being a Monte Carlo method, its performance is dependent on the variance of sampled quantities and variance reduction methods are crucial for the challenges posed by ever denser process technologies and layout-dependent effects. In this work, we present a novel, universal variance reduction method for floating random walk-based capacitance extraction, which is conceptually simple, highly efficient and provably reduces variance in all extractions, especially when layout-dependent effects are present. It is complementary to existing mathematical formulations for variance reduction and its performance gains are experienced on top of theirs. Numerical experiments demonstrate substantial such gains of up to 50% in number of walks necessary as well as in actual extraction times compared to the best previously proposed variance reduction approaches for the floating random-walk.

items.abstract_text: Clock meshes are widely used in high-performance VLSI systems to minimize skew and tolerate On-Chip Variation (OCV) in nanometer technologies. However, analyzing meshes is difficult because reconvergent paths and multi-source drivers prevent static timing analysis (STA) tools from handling mesh loops, making SPICE the industrial standard. SPICE simulations are accurate but slow, so clock-mesh synthesis relies on approximate models that overlook critical effects such as non-linear buffer driving caused by input slew and input skew. We propose a Graph Neural Network (GNN) based surrogate model of the clock mesh with a new graph representation and a new architecture that predicts power while also improving the delay and slew predictions at the sinks and capturing the skew histogram under OCV. Trained on SPICE data and tested on unseen real designs, our model achieves average errors of $3.40$~ps in delay, $4.14$~ps in slew and $4.46$~ps in skew, compared with $6.28$~ps, $12.35$~ps, and $11.62$~ps for our prior model, and $74.37$~ps delay and $27.51$~ps skew for the approximate method used in current state-of-the-art works. Our model predicts power within $3.4\%$ of SPICE on average, while delivering $18\times$-$1706\times$ speed-ups over the approximate method under OCV modeling, enabling faster and more accurate clock-mesh design-space exploration. A case study on a real design further shows that our surrogate model finds buffering candidates that, at a balanced tradeoff, improves $99^{\text{th}}$-percentile skew by $49.1\%$, reduces power by $25.7\%$, and reduces area by $37.3\%$ at the cost of a $6.8\%$ increase in $99^{\text{th}}$-percentile maximum slew as compared to the state-of-the-art work.

items.abstract_text: Modern FPGA SoCs are no longer just collections of accelerators on top of a programmable fabric. They combine programmable logic with hardened processors, NoCs, and components that dominate end-to-end performance. Evaluating individual pieces is insufficient; system performance depends on the interplay of SoC components. However, current FPGA SoC simulations provide limited support for this style of evaluation. Vendor simulations capture these interactions but are prohibitively slow for iterative design-space exploration. At the same time, generic software models overly abstract the hardware components that determine real behavior, resulting in less accurate simulations. Fast, easy-to-use simulators that accurately model real SoCs are critical for system debugging and design space exploration. We present Naviq, an open-source, cycle-level software simulator for FPGA SoCs, tuned to AMD Versal-class architectures. Naviq bridges accurate but slow vendor simulation and fast software modeling: it captures key behaviors of modern commercial FPGA SoCs while being fast enough for debugging and design-space exploration. Naviq models hardened SoC infrastructure in C++ and integrates accelerators through Verilator, allowing designers to evaluate custom hardware in a full-system environment. At the center of Naviq is an AXI4-compliant NoC model that captures transaction ordering, packetization, routing, backpressure, and memory interactions. Naviq provides CPU and memory integration, protocol checking, checkpointing, tracing, and performance-analysis tools for debugging and design-space exploration. Experimental results show Naviq closely reproduces the bandwidth and latency of Vivado's RTL NoC model while accelerating the evaluated simulations by 81x-182x. We present five case studies demonstrating Naviq's capabilities. Naviq enables practical full-system evaluation of modern FPGA SoC designs.

items.abstract_text: Global routing is a fundamental issue in the design of electronic circuits, as it directly relates to the efficiency, reliability, and compactness of the overall layout of integrated systems. As the demand for higher functionality and reliability within a limited chip area increases, the importance of routing as a design consideration has never been greater. Efficient global routing optimization techniques are therefore required to connect all pins with minimal wirelength (WL), while avoiding congestion and interference across multiple nets within the design space. As the number of nets to be routed increases, global routing inherently suffers from a combinatorial explosion in the design space, making it increasingly difficult to obtain feasible solutions. In this paper, we focus on solving constrained global routing problems based on a heuristic A*-based framework. Based on this concept, a hybrid approach is proposed by integrating constrained A* with flow matching (FM). The method utilizes FM to construct a global cost map that captures routing tendencies across the design space, which is then used to guide the constrained A* search process. This enables efficient exploration of the solution space while satisfying routing constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable WL and via usage to baseline methods while maintaining constraint satisfaction across a wide range of scenarios. Notably, the framework shows strong capability in solving complex routing instances that are difficult to handle using conventional approaches. Additionally, the method shows robust generalization performance across different problem sizes and net configurations.

To maintain power integrity, a large copper-filled area is used for power delivery in package substrate design. Since multiple power domains share the same substrate metal layer, the layer must be partitioned into several non-overlapping sub-regions, which engineers manually handcraft. In this article, we propose an automated framework for power plane layout partitioning and optimization. The framework comprises two major stages: topology generation and polygon generation. In the topology generation stage, we propose pin grouping, edge selection, and edge-cost adjustment methods to efficiently generate the topology of each power domain within the same metal layer. In the polygon generation stage, pseudo-node insertion is first applied to generate initial metal polygons, and a bisection method is then iteratively performed to optimize the shapes, areas, and resistances of the multiple power domains simultaneously. The experimental results demonstrate that our framework efficiently generates power plane layouts that account for static power integrity (DC IR-drop) and can serve as a basis for future transient analysis.

As the scale of circuit design increases, automatic placement and routing (P&R) become crucial for optimizing device performance and ensuring scalable fabrication. Previous algorithms face challenges in solving large-scale placement and routing problems with the current clocking scheme. In this article, a novel approach is proposed to decouple the placement and routing issues in the design of FCN logic circuits. By adopting a layered method, the issues are confined within each layer, and long wires between layers are eliminated while reducing crossovers through node sorting. A* algorithm is employed to solve the routing between logic gates, and an innovative clock allocation mechanism ensures clock synchronization. A standard cell library is used to implement the mapping of an FCN circuit from a gate-level layout to a nanocell-level layout. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared with state-of-the-art approaches such as fiction, Ropper, and genetic algorithms (GA). Specifically, it achieves higher success rates, fewer gates and faster execution times, along with lower delays–while also delivering reduced area overhead, particularly when compared with Ropper and GA. Furthermore, this article achieves automatic placement and routing of FCN circuits with over 1000 nodes, making it more suitable for large-scale FCN circuit design.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven electronic design automation (EDA) techniques have been extensively explored for VLSI circuit design applications. Most recently, foundation AI models for circuits have emerged as a new technology trend. Unlike traditional task-specific AI solutions, these new AI models are developed through two stages: (1) self-supervised pre-training on a large amount of unlabeled data to learn intrinsic circuit properties; and (2) efficient fine-tuning for specific downstream applications, such as early-stage design quality evaluation, circuit-related context generation, and functional verification. This new paradigm brings many advantages: model generalization, less reliance on labeled circuit data, efficient adaptation to new tasks, and unprecedented generative capability. In this article, we propose referring to AI models developed with this new paradigm as circuit foundation models (CFMs) . This article provides a comprehensive survey of the latest progress in circuit foundation models, unprecedentedly covering over 160 relevant works. Over 90% of our introduced works were published in or after 2022, indicating that this emerging research trend has attracted wide attention in a short period. In this survey, we propose to categorize all existing circuit foundation models into two primary types: (1) encoder-based methods performing general circuit representation learning for predictive tasks ; and (2) decoder-based methods leveraging large language models (LLMs) for generative tasks . For our introduced works, we cover their input modalities, model architecture, pre-training strategies, domain adaptation techniques, and downstream design applications. In addition, this article discussed the unique properties of circuits from the data perspective. These circuit properties have motivated many works in this domain and differentiated them from general AI techniques. Finally, we shared our observed challenges and potential future research directions about developing foundation AI models for EDA methodologies.

items.title: Two-for-One: Image-based Transformations to Mitigate Adversarial Attacks and Random Faults at Once in Safety-critical AI Systems
items.journal: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.venue_name: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.summary: Dual Modular Redundancy (DMR) and Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR) are commonly used methods for providing fault detection and/or tolerance in safety-critical systems by incorporating redundant – and often diverse – components. However, these systems can still be susceptible to adversarial attacks that may deceive AI models, potentially leading to severe consequences. In this article, we introduce enhanced DMR and TMR strategies for image-based object detection, leveraging image transformations during inference to help reduce the impact of adversarial inputs, while preserving the inherent advantages of diverse redundancy for safety purposes. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves robustness under adversarial conditions, achieving up to 12.9% and 12.2% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art solutions in DMR and TMR configurations, respectively, when attacks are individually crafted for each image. Furthermore, against universal adversarial attacks, our solution achieves even greater accuracy gains, with up to 26.8% and 26.0% higher accuracy in DMR and TMR configurations, respectively.

items.abstract_text: As demand for semiconductor talent grows, education must prepare learners for the complexity of modern chip design. Instruction typically relies on lectures, textbooks, software exercises, and limited laboratory experiences. Although foundational, these approaches offer limited support for understanding the spatial, multi-scale, and interconnected nature of chip design. Virtual reality (VR) can help learners visualize and interact with complex structures and processes, but its educational opportunities remain underexplored. We examined this gap through chip design curriculum analysis and semi-structured interviews with five participants representing instructional and learner perspectives. We characterized four learning demands: descriptive knowledge, procedural knowledge, relational and design-focused reasoning, and strategic decision-making. We identified challenges in connecting abstraction levels, interpreting spatial structures and temporal behavior, bridging theory and practice, and reasoning about design trade-offs and downstream consequences. Drawing on these findings and prior research, we mapped learning demands to six immersive affordances: spatial visualization, multi-scale navigation, interactive manipulation, temporal dynamics visualization, immediate feedback, and collaboration. These findings motivate Cross-Scale Spatial Reasoning (CSSR) as a conceptual lens for understanding how learners connect physical structures, design representations, and engineering consequences across the chip design pipeline. We contribute an empirically informed account of learning challenges, a structured mapping of learning demands to immersive affordances, and concrete design opportunities for immersive semiconductor education. These contributions guide the development and evaluation of immersive environments that support reasoning across scales, representations, and design processes.

items.title: Challenges in the verification of MOSAIX ASIC for ALICE ITS3
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: The MOSAIX is a wafer-scale, full-functionality prototype ASIC for the ALICE Inner Tracking System (ITS3) upgrade, implemented in $65\,\text{nm}$ stitching technology. It integrates 144 independently powered pixel matrices, eight $10\,\text{Gb/s}$ serializers, and on-chip data and power distribution, making full-chip verification highly resource-intensive (over $80\,\text{GB}$ of memory and 192,000 tests). Verification also targets a sophisticated power-up sequence and radiation conditions of $10^{6}$\ particles $s^{-1} cm^{-2}$ and $4\,\text{kGy}$ TID. This work presents a UVM-based verification strategy that identified 260 design errors and summarizes key lessons from ASIC sign-off.

items.abstract_text: Generative models are increasingly used for circuit synthesis and optimization by proposing topologies, sizing devices, and exploring large design spaces. We investigate whether they can instead support design discovery, where generated structures must depart from known designs while producing reproducible electrical behavior. We propose Delta-Seeker, a closed-loop circuit search framework that combines discrete diffusion for topology generation and mutation with structural checking, SPICE-in-the-loop sizing, Pareto selection, and feedback from prior search outcomes. The search controller uses progress and recurring structural failures to allocate evaluation effort and steer subsequent topology generation, while independent re-sizing and operating-corner analysis are performed only after search. In generator-only experiments, cross-generation feedback increases structurally valid children from 143 to 945 and reduces the faulty-candidate fraction from 0.925 to 0.761. In op-amp topology discovery at matched sizing cost, Delta-Seeker yields 54 designs that remain feasible in at least three of four independent re-sizings and 18 that additionally pass device-level checks and supply-temperature corner analysis, compared with 38 and 10 under fixed control. Removing cross-generation memory reduces independently robust discoveries from 54 to 43 and seven-corner robust discoveries from 40 to 27. In DC-DC converter search, nearest-parent analysis identifies a corpus-absent topology whose generated switching current path changes its nearest training-corpus parent from infeasible at all four operating corners to feasible at all four, while increasing median efficiency from 31.2% to 98.96%. These results show that closed-loop generative search can support circuit discovery beyond structural novelty by identifying new topologies with independently verified changes in circuit operation.

items.title: RTL-Interact: Training EDA-Interactive Models for Multi-Task RTL Design
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: Large language models offer a promising route to register-transfer-level (RTL) design, but reliable implementations require checking and revision based on electronic design automation (EDA) tools' feedback. Existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such EDA tools or rely on separate generation and repair components. We introduce RTL-Interact, a multi-task post-training framework that trains a single RTL-specialized model to generate RTL, construct task-appropriate EDA checks, and revise implementations using tool feedback. The framework combines automatically constructed multi-task demonstrations with staged supervision from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning. We further introduce Pattern-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) for multi-task reinforcement learning. PAPO augments Group Relative Policy Optimization with correctness-gated rewards that favor concise successful checking while rewarding effective revision, and uses task grouping to preserve coverage across objectives. On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B achieves 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5, surpassing its teacher model, DeepSeek-V3.2, while RTL-Interact-8B achieves 44.9% weighted Pass@1. A

Existing RTL-specialized models often lack learned interaction with such EDA tools or rely on separate generation and repair components. We introduce RTL-Interact, a multi-task post-training framework that trains a single RTL-specialized model to generate RTL, construct task-appropriate EDA checks, and revise implementations using tool feedback. The framework combines automatically constructed multi-task demonstrations with staged supervision from chain-of-thought to tool-integrated reasoning. We further introduce Pattern-Aware Policy Optimization (PAPO) for multi-task reinforcement learning. PAPO augments Group Relative Policy Optimization with correctness-gated rewards that favor concise successful checking while rewarding effective revision, and uses task grouping to preserve coverage across objectives. On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B achieves 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5, surpassing its teacher model, DeepSeek-V3.2, while RTL-Interact-8B achieves 44.9% weighted Pass@1. Additionally, we show that PAPO can reduce average tool calls by 63.8% while improving Pass@1. Both models also outperform all RTL-specialized baselines on VerilogEval v2 and RTLLM v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method.

items.title: A flexible electronics and DAQ system for the Timepix4 ASIC
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: The INFN Data Acquisition system (IDAQ) is designed for data-driven readout of the Timepix4 ASIC, supporting simultaneous time-of-arrival and time-over-threshold measurements with nanosecond precision. The system architecture combines dedicated hardware for high-speed serial data transmission, FPGA-based data processing, and a Trigger Logic Unit for synchronization and timing distribution. It operates in continuous streaming and triggered modes, ensuring low-latency and high-throughput performance. The system has been deployed in test-beam campaigns within the 4DPHOTON project, demonstrating stable operation, precise timing alignment, and reliable data handling under high-rate conditions.

items.journal: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.venue_name: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
items.summary: Lithography hotspot detection is essential for ensuring yield and reliability in integrated circuit manufacturing. However, existing approaches typically analyze small layout clips in isolation, resulting in inefficient and fragmented detection workflows. In this work, we propose a novel formulation of hotspot detection as a point cloud classification problem and introduce a tailored neural network architecture based on submanifold sparse convolution to efficiently process large layouts. Our method operates directly on polygon segments used in mask optimization, enabling fine-grained predictions aligned with downstream hotspot fixing. By representing layouts as point clouds and leveraging the sparsity of the data, our approach supports large-scale detection with a single forward pass, improving runtime over the compared clip-based methods. items.abstract_text: High-level synthesis (HLS) expedites accelerator customization by delivering a high-level hardware programming paradigm and offering a rich set of optimization directives. However, the quality of HLS designs is highly dependent on the designers’ selection of directives in the trade-off between different design metrics, which is non-trivial and can lead to a large design turnaround time. Design space exploration (DSE) serves as a promising solution to this problem, but existing studies on DSE suffer from a lack of scalability for large-scale applications and often spend a substantial portion of the exploration budget on costly design points. To address this problem, this paper proposes AutoShrink 2.0 , a DSE engine that adaptively shrinks the large search space of an HLS design to gradually retain only high-quality solutions. AutoShrink 2.0 incorporates (1) a comprehensive design space pruning strategy that integrates the joint effect of directives and domain knowledge, (2) an importance-guided Pareto optimization algorithm which dynamically traces the importance ranking of the applied directives and leverages this ranking to navigate the search direction of Pareto frontiers, and (3) a cost-aware post-filtering mechanism to screen out candidates that are computationally expensive yet of limited gain, reducing runtime overhead within a single evaluation. Experimental results on Vitis HLS demonstrate that AutoShrink 2.0 achieves an average distance to reference set (ADRS) of 8.40% across multiple applications with design spaces containing up to \(\text{10}^\text{16} \) design points, outperforming three heuristic methods and three state-of-the-art approaches by 8.01 × and 6.24 ×, respectively. On timeout-prone benchmarks, the cost-aware post-filtering strategy reduces the average timeout ratio by 66.1% compared with the variant without this strategy. Furthermore, design tool transfer experiments from Vitis HLS to Catapult HLS demonstrate the promising cross-tool applicability of AutoShrink 2.0.

items.abstract_text: Recently, the use of large language models (LLMs) for Verilog code generation has attracted great research interest to enable hardware design automation. However, previous works have shown a gap between the ability of LLMs and the practical demands of hardware description language (HDL) engineering. This gap includes differences in how engineers phrase questions and hallucinations in the generated code. To address these challenges, we introduce HaVen , a novel LLM framework designed to mitigate hallucinations and align Verilog code generation with the practices of HDL engineers. HaVen tackles hallucination issues by proposing a comprehensive taxonomy and employing a chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism to translate symbolic modalities ( e .g. truth tables, state diagrams, e tc.) into accurate natural language descriptions. Furthermore, HaVen bridges this gap by using a data augmentation strategy, synthesizing high-quality instruction-code pairs that match real HDL engineering practices. Building upon HaVen , we develop HaVen -R, a reasoning-augmented extension fine-tuned with a Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT) Dataset and a Reasoning Dataset, enabling Chain-of-Thought (CoT) guided self-reflection to iteratively repair Verilog code. We further introduce HaVen -Agent, a multi-agent system that orchestrates a Planner Agent (GPT-4o), a Coder Agent ( HaVen -R), and a Verifier Agent for iterative code repair. Our experiments demonstrate that HaVen -Agent significantly improves the correctness of Verilog code generation, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on VerilogEval and RTLLM benchmarks. Additional evaluations include a 400-case multi-generator repair study, component and iteration ablations, CVDP, end-to-end cost and latency analysis, and protocol-aware comparisons with recent feedback, agentic, and reasoning-augmented methods. HaVen is publicly available at https://github.com/Intelligent-Computing-Research-Group/HaVen.

items.title: GI-RTL-Fuzz: Grammar-Informed RTL Generation with LLMs for End-to-End Differential Simulator Fuzzing
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: Register-Transfer Level (RTL) simulators are fundamental to modern IC design workflows, yet like any complex software, they frequently contain critical bugs that compromise simulation accuracy. To systematically stress-test these tools, we introduce GI-RTL-Fuzz, a grammar-informed fuzzing framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate high-quality RTL test cases. Our key innovation is guiding the LLM's generation process using Backus-Naur Form (BNF) grammar coverage information, enabling the exploration of complex and rarely-tested language features. By performing differential testing against different RTL simulators, our framework uncovered a significant number of previously unknown inconsistencies in both the linting process and simulation results of major Verilog simulators.

items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: Physical non-idealities in integrated circuit (IC) design, fabrication, and operation are concealed by conventional hardware abstractions, causing unexpected performance variations in kernels. items.abstract_text: Physical non-idealities in integrated circuit (IC) design, fabrication, and operation are concealed by conventional hardware abstractions, causing unexpected performance variations in kernels. For large-scale workloads, such as AI training and inference, performance unpredictability can lead to substantial losses. We investigate this problem in NVIDIA H100 GPUs with their distributed shared memory (DSMEM) architectural feature that reduces data movement from the L2 cache to Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) with multicast loads, and uncover that floorsweeping restricts the number of SMs usable for clustered execution, increasing the number of execution waves of kernels. To alleviate this performance penalty, we introduce the wave-aware clustering strategy that accounts for these resource constraints and improves the throughput of the Hopper version of FlashAttention 4 by up to 5.30% over the unclustered baseline. Furthermore, we discover that the power constraint imposed by the thermal design power (TDP) limit causes the DSMEM-based memory bandwidth optimization to improve the throughput even for compute-bound kernels by creating a power headroom for higher SM frequencies through reduced data movement. Extending this analysis beyond GPUs, we find that power constraints also limit throughput scaling on Tenstorrent's Wormhole accelerator, highlighting the broader importance of accounting for physical non-idealities in kernel performance engineering.

items.title: Back-End-Of-Line Integration of 2-Terminal Ferroelectric Hafnia Synaptic Weights on Commercial CMOS Process
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: Functionalising the back-end-of-line (BEOL) of CMOS with emerging materials is a key route to neural network accelerators and neuromorphic systems. In this work, we demonstrate for the first time the integration of 2-terminal ferroelectric synaptic weights in the BEOL of as-delivered commercial 180 nm CMOS dies. A novel material stack is proposed, in which a WOx/[HfO2-ZrO2] bilayer is sandwiched between TiN and Mo electrodes. For devices annealed at 450 °C, programming below 1.8 V is achieved with a cycle-to-cycle variation below 3 %. Synaptic weights annealed at 500 °C exhibit more gradual weight updates, while the tested underlying NMOS transistors remain functional after the complete integration process. The trade-off between thermal budget and on-device training performance is illustrated using hardware-aware neural network simulations.

items.title: Multimode continuous-variable quantum key distribution with CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic integration
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: Multiplexing and photonic-electronic integration offer a route to scalable and high-throughput quantum key distribution (QKD) networks through parallel transmission and compact hardware suited to volume manufacturing. Realizing this route requires multichannel transmitters and receivers, and a security analysis accounting for mode coupling. Here we present a CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic multimode continuous-variable QKD architecture, using polarization multiplexing as a two-mode example. Silicon-photonic transmitter and receiver chips prepare and detect two polarization modes in parallel. The receiver is co-integrated with a dual-channel 28-nm CMOS transimpedance amplifier, providing shot-noise clearances exceeding 20 dB in both channels. Pilot-assisted unitary digital recovery removes the need for active optical polarization control, while a multimode security analysis accounts for the mode crosstalk. At 2 percent residual crosstalk, the multimode analysis extends the simulated secure distance from 39 to 84 km, near the crosstalk-free limit of 89 km. items.abstract_text: Multiplexing and photonic-electronic integration offer a route to scalable and high-throughput quantum key distribution (QKD) networks through parallel transmission and compact hardware suited to volume manufacturing. Realizing this route requires multichannel transmitters and receivers, and a security analysis accounting for mode coupling. Here we present a CMOS-compatible photonic-electronic multimode continuous-variable QKD architecture, using polarization multiplexing as a two-mode example. Silicon-photonic transmitter and receiver chips prepare and detect two polarization modes in parallel. The receiver is co-integrated with a dual-channel 28-nm CMOS transimpedance amplifier, providing shot-noise clearances exceeding 20 dB in both channels. Pilot-assisted unitary digital recovery removes the need for active optical polarization control, while a multimode security analysis accounts for the mode crosstalk. At 2 percent residual crosstalk, the multimode analysis extends the simulated secure distance from 39 to 84 km, near the crosstalk-free limit of 89 km. Over 10 km of deployed fibre, the mean total finite-size secret-key rate estimate is 6.69 Mbit/s, 12 percent above the single-mode analysis from the same digitally recovered data. These results establish a route to scalable multimode quantum-secured networks built on technology suited to mass production.

items.abstract_text: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved Verilog generation. However, most training pipelines distill natural-language reasoning traces whose intermediate design decisions are weakly structured and are primarily selected according to the correctness of the final generated RTL. We present MCTS-SFT, a verifier-guided framework for curating reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Verilog generation models. MCTS-SFT formulates trace construction as search over intermediate reasoning states and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to propagate functional feedback from complete Verilog rollouts to earlier design decisions. Within this framework, we introduce Plan-MCTS, which searches over compact hardware-design plans that explicitly represent interfaces, timing, state, behavior, and update rules. We further study plan-preserving supervision, in which the searched structured state is retained as part of the downstream SFT target. Our experiments find that Plan-MCTS achieves the highest functional trace yield, with 84.2% correct traces compared with 81.9% for one-shot structured planning and 82.0% for unguided tree exploration. For identical Plan-MCTS trajectories and Verilog outputs, retaining the explicit searched plan during SFT raises pass@10 from 52.56% to 57.7%, demonstrating that the representation of intermediate design decisions materially affects downstream learning. In a separate 6,000-trace study, MCTS-curated supervision improves pass@10 over full-response chain-of-thought distillation by up to 3.7 points while reducing downstream generation length by approximately 50% on VerilogEval-v2. These results demonstrate that structured hardware planning, verifier-guided search, and explicit intermediate-state supervision provide complementary mechanisms for constructing more effective and token-efficient training data for Verilog generation.

items.abstract_text: The realm of high-performance computing has expanded to include machine learning tasks of many forms. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are becoming increasingly popular, with their applications expanding across diverse domains. As the scale of graph data continues to grow, including larger numbers of nodes, edges, and higher embedding dimensions, standardized libraries such as DGL and PyG have been developed to facilitate GNN computation. These libraries allow the computation to be described a a high level of abstraction, providing high productivity on the part of the developer. However, with the rapid increase in the number of processor cores and the evolution of multicore architectures, these libraries often show poor scalability and fail to execute GNN inference efficiently on the latest multicore systems, particularly those with upwards of a hundred cores. To address this limitation, we introduce FrontGI, a fast and scalable set of techniques that advances the frontier of GNN inference on large-scale graphs (over 100,000 vertices) by leveraging graph-property- and architecture-aware design. FrontGI employs different parallelization strategies optimized for diverse graph structures, maximizing the utilization of multi-level cache hierarchies in multicore systems. We evaluate a number of GNN models with FrontGI on a 128-core AMD EPYC system. Compared to state-of-the-art libraries, FrontGI achieves up to 3.35$\times$, 3.20$\times$, 2.89$\times$ and 3.10$\times$ speedups over DGL for GCN, GraphSAGE, GIN, and SGC models, respectively, and even greater improvements over PyG, across a range of large-scale, high-dimensional graph datasets with diverse structural properties.

items.abstract_text: Cybersecurity education has predominantly focused on software and network security, under the assumption that the underlying hardware is trustworthy. Threats introduced through the global semiconductor supply chain, together with vulnerabilities arising during design and integration, challenge the assumption that hardware can serve as an unquestioned root of trust. Sensor-enabled systems and machine-learning accelerators further expand the hardware attack surface. The undergraduate curriculum of electrical and computer engineering and computer science programs has not evolved accordingly. Core courses cover the design and the functionality of hardware while the security aspects remain overlooked, and dedicated hardware security (HS) courses are elective, scarce, and often restricted to graduate students. At the University of Florida, fewer than 7% of the undergraduate electrical and computer engineering students register for the introductory HS course each year. We present an integrated and economical approach that disseminates fundamental HS concepts within existing core courses through contextual learning. Nine hands-on modules were developed such that each security concept exercises an associated design concept of the core course, as a component of that course and not as a course of their own. Doing the security work is how the student exercises the design topic, so the modules are built to strengthen the host course and not only to add to it. Three were assessed across three offerings of the embedded systems course through one course survey and two conducted by an external evaluator, with 25 respondents. We report what those instruments measured and the limitations of the approach.

items.title: Development of an FPGA-Based Readout System and Functional Characterization of a Custom NSX1 ASIC for X-ray instrumentation
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: We developed an FPGA-based readout system for a front-end ASIC (NSX1) with 64 channels to read out a large- area silicon drift detector used in X-ray detection instruments such as the Wide Field Monitor module for the STROBE-X mission concept. The FPGA acts as a central controller for the NSX1 configuration, implementing trigger handling and event sequencing, precise event timestamping, control of an external ADC for digitization, and data transfer to the host PC. The system enables comprehensive ASIC characterization; here, we demonstrate preliminary ASIC functionality and characterization tests using a calibrated pulser for two programmable linear gain responses of 375 mV/fC and 750 mV/fC. These preliminary results validate the low-noise performance of the NSX1 ASIC and demonstrate successful integration of the DAQ system.

items.title: Embodied Emissions of 2.5D and 3D Scaling in Chipletized GPUs for Low-Carbon AI
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: GPU compute resources are scaling to support growing AI workloads, leading to further rises in the climate change impact of hyperscale data centers that rely on high-performance GPUs. To model how packaging decisions impact the carbon footprint we have estimated the embodied emissions (EE) of a chiplet-based GPU that has been scaled in 2.5D and 3D using the imec.netzero modelling platform. We doubled the number of compute units and high bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity in the 2.5D and 3D scaled systems and found that 3D scaling results in an 89% increase in EE, as compared to an increase of 141% for 2.5D scaling, positioning 3D scaling as an attractive solution to limit the embodied emissions due to GPU scaling.

items.title: Development of an Analog Front-End Using NINO ASIC for Mini-ICAL
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: The mini-ICAL was supposed to be a pre-prototype detector of the Iron CALorimeter (ICAL) of the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) project. Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) was the active element of these detectors. As this detector operates in avalanche mode, one needs a very fast pre-amplifier for signal processing. NINO ASIC developed for the ALICE time-of-flight detector was a potential chip to be used as the analog-front end. This paper presents an 8-in-1 pre-amplifier board developed using the NINO ASIC, a single-ended to differential signal conversion using the differential driver chip manufactured by Texas Instruments, production of the boards, lessons learned during production, testing of these boards, and interface with RPCs. Finally, its performance based on strip rates and efficiency of the detector will also be discussed.

items.title: GTX: Graph Transformer for Parasitic EXtraction on Analog Circuits
items.venue_name: Proceedings of the 63rd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference
items.summary: We present GTX, a graph-transformer-based framework for accurate parasitic prediction in analog circuits. GTX combines a customized parasitic modeling scheme with HGNNs and global attention to capture both local device interactions and long-range interconnect dependencies. Experiments show GTX achieves higher prediction accuracy than prior ML-based methods and generates predicted-parasitics netlists whose post-layout simulations closely match commercial parasitic-extracted netlists. Moreover, parasitic inference is 232.7× faster than commercial PEX, and simulations using predicted-parasitics netlists are up to 8.4× faster while closely matching the results of commercial parasitic-extracted netlists, demonstrating GTX's effectiveness in accelerating layout-aware analog design.

items.title: MBA: Mega-Buffer Architecture Based on 1T1C IGZO eDRAM for Efficient LLM Inference
items.venue_name: Proceedings of the 63rd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference
items.summary: Substantial weight and KV cache transfers between the GPU and HBM severely constrain Large Language Model (LLM) inference system performance. While LLM compression techniques can reduce memory footprint and transfer volume, existing methods are often task-specific and compromise model accuracy. This work proposes a mega-buffer architecture (MBA) that integrates gigabyte-scale on-chip buffers utilizing the embedded DRAM (eDRAM) technology recently introduced by TSMC. To fully leverage this large on-chip memory, we introduce a KV cache prioritized mapping (KVP) scheme that minimizes inefficient KV cache traffic between the HBM and the chip. Furthermore, a highly efficient pipeline integrating double buffering mechanism (DB) is co-designed with an iteration-aware eviction strategy (IA) to enhance data reuse and sustain high compute utilization. Evaluation results show that MBA attains 5.99x and 3.63x end-to-end speedup, and 8.86x and 4.93x energy efficiency improvement against GPU and LLM accelerator baselines, demonstrating a highly efficient architectural solution for LLM inference.

items.title: UVMarvel: an Automated LLM-aided UVM Machine for Subsystem-level RTL Verification
items.venue_name: Proceedings of the 63rd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference
items.summary: Verification presents a major bottleneck in Integrated Circuit (IC) development, consuming nearly 70% of total effort. While the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) improves reuse through structured verification environments, constructing subsystem-level UVM testbenches and generating high-quality stimuli still require extensive manual coding, repeated EDA tool runs, and deep protocol and micro-architectural expertise. We present UVMarvel, an automated verification framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to build UVM testbenches for subsystem-level RTL. UVMarvel introduces an Intermediate Representation (IR) and a Bus Protocol Library to translate heterogeneous specifications into protocol-correct subsystem-level UVM testbenches, and employs a Signal Tracker and a Verilog Patching Library to guide LLM-based stimuli refinement. UVMarvel is the first framework capable of automatically constructing subsystem-level UVM testbenches across mainstream bus protocols, and it achieves an average code coverage of 95.65%, while reducing verification time from several human working days to a 4.5-hour automated execution.

items.title: SVACoder: Training Specialized LLMs for Hardware Assertion Generation via RTL-Grounded Bidirectional Data Synthesis
items.venue_name: Proceedings of the 63rd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference
items.summary: SystemVerilog Assertions (SVAs) are crucial for hardware verification. Recent studies leverage general-purpose LLMs to translate natural language properties to SVAs (NL2SVA), but they perform poorly due to limited data. We propose a data synthesis framework to tackle two challenges: the scarcity of high-quality real-world SVA corpora and the lack of reliable methods to determine NL-SVA semantic equivalence. For the former, large-scale open-source RTLs are used to guide LLMs to generate real-world SVAs; for the latter, bidirectional translation serves as a data selection method. With the synthesized data, we train SVACoder, a series of SVA generation models. Notably, SVACoder-14B achieves 75.8% on NL2SVA-Human and 84.0% on NL2SVA-Machine in Func.@1, matching or exceeding advanced LLMs like GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1.

items.title: DeTrojan: Detecting Trojan Circuits Using a Purpose-Built Graph Neural Network with Community-Enhanced Classification
items.venue_name: Proceedings of the 63rd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference
items.summary: Gate-level Hardware Trojan (HT) detection using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often suffers from limited accuracy due to the reliance on structure-only features and fragmented node-level predictions. We propose a GNN-based framework, DeTrojan, to overcome these challenges through three key innovations: (1) functionality-aware feature engineering, (2) an edge-aware GNN architecture with Jumping Knowledge and global context aggregation, and (3) accurate Trojan circuit localization with community-aware classification refinement. Evaluated on the 2025 ICCAD CAD Contest Hardware Trojan benchmarks, DeTrojan achieves a 16.6% improvement in circuit-level prediction accuracy and a 47.3% relative increase in gate-level F1-score over the state-of-the-art machine learning (ML)-based methods. Furthermore, incorporating our proposed features and refinement modules into the existing approaches yield up to a 10.5% gain in accuracy and a 50.8% increase in the F1-score, demonstrating the effectiveness and generality of our framework. Notably, DeTrojan secured first place in the 2025 ICCAD CAD Contest and will be open-sourced to facilitate further research.

items.title: UNCHARTED: A Universal Circuit Design Hierarchical Model based on Auto-Regressive Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network with Exogenous Driving Inputs
items.venue_name: Proceedings of the 63rd ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference
items.summary: Analog circuit design is time-consuming and heavily dependent on the expertise of human designers. This paper presents a universal circuit design hierarchical model (UNCHARTED). It is the first machine learning-based framework that emulates transient simulation by modeling physical behaviors of individual circuit components through the graph neural network. The sizing of circuit elements is reflected through low-rank adaptation, and inverse design is achieved by the back-propagation mechanism. UNCHARTED can accelerate simulation by up to 241.9x, with high similarity (>95%) to SPICE simulation in more than 70% of tested circuits. Inverse design examples of a delay chain and an amplifier also demonstrate its powerful capabilities in automatic design optimization.

items.abstract_text: Field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based emulation delivers orders of magnitude higher throughput than software simulation. However, fundamental clocking differences between application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) and FPGAs limit its performance and capacity. To address this, we model the sampling of all flip-flops (FFs), originally triggered by multiple generated clocks, as an ordered sequence of events and reproduce their behavior at each emulation step. We introduce two clock models. The output-gated model (M o ) samples the clock, input, and output of each FF, requiring more logic resources but no event ordering. Conversely, the sampling-gated model (M s ) uses clock edge detection to conditionally sample, using fewer logic resources but requiring event ordering. We then adopt a hybrid strategy that applies M o to clock-generation logic to avoid resolving complex clock dependencies, and applies M s to the data path to save logic resources. We formally prove that the transformed design is sequentially equivalent to the original at every emulation step. We propose matching-point inductive verification (MPIV), which augments the inductive proof with matching points recorded during the transformation and reduces verification tasks to satisfiability (SAT) checks. Across industrial designs with up to 11,515 generated clocks, the hybrid approach incurs modest overhead (1.7% FFs and 5.8% lookup tables (LUTs) on average). MPIV achieves up to 2,950 × speedup and succeeds on large designs where a widely used model checker ABC-PDR times out. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first publicly documented and formally verified methodology for eliminating logic-generated clocks in ASIC-to-FPGA emulation.

items.abstract_text: In recent years, a novel non-invasive laser-assisted attack known as Optical Probing (OP) has been demonstrated to effectively probe the internal state of integrated circuits. This attack exploits the relative transparency of the silicon substrate to Near-InfraRed (NIR) light, enabling optical access through the backside of the chip. Consequently, OP poses a significant threat to information processed or stored on the chip and may facilitate Intellectual Property (IP) theft or reverse engineering. Existing mitigation techniques can be broadly classified into three categories: (1) fabrication-level modifications, (2) sensor-based countermeasures, and (3) circuit-level design techniques. Fabrication-based countermeasures are costly and often incompatible with standard industrial manufacturing processes, limiting their practicality for OP-resilient chip design. Sensor-based countermeasures may be circumvented by adaptive attackers, whereas circuit-level techniques typically require modifications to the layout of standard-cell libraries. Such modifications are time-consuming and can introduce considerable PPA overheads relative to conventional standard-cell designs. Therefore, this study investigates whether increasing the local layout density around a target logic cell can enhance resilience against OP attacks without requiring modifications beyond the layout level. In this context, local density refers to the fraction of a predefined region surrounding the target cell that is occupied by neighboring logic cells and associated layout structures. Our methodology employs standard logic cells to protect the chip’s sensitive information from an adversary equipped with OP capabilities. We found that increasing the local density of surrounding logic cells near a target logic cell enhances overall reflection, effectively masking the reflection from the target logic cell. This can significantly improve the concealment of the secure cell’s information from the OP attack since the reflections from the neighboring logic cells overlap with the target logic cells that need to be secured. Hence, an adversary cannot distinguish the exact location of the source of reflection. We demonstrate that this methodology can effectively countermeasure against OP attacks by conducting detailed experiments on the relationship between density and reflection, using NAND, INVERTER, NOR, and Flip-Flop cells. We exhaustively evaluated thousands of placement strategies with varying densities to show the efficacy of our technique against OP attacks. Moreover, we demonstrate the integration of our OP attack mitigation technique into the ASIC flow for designing an AES-128 core. We demonstrate that our technique in the worst-case comes with a 1% increase in power consumption, a 1% increase in area, and no change in the operating frequency compared to the unprotected AES-128 core against OP attack.

items.abstract_text: Cytokine-mediated inflammation disorders such as sepsis and cytokine release syndrome demand bedside multiplex panels that resolve pro- and anti-inflammatory dynamics in minutes, yet label-free FET cytokine sensors remain limited to few devices, single analytes, and PDMS packaging that sorbs small molecules and leaches oligomers. We present a CMOS platform pairing a 128 x 128 ion-sensitive field-effect transistor (ISFET) array (SkyWater 130 nm, SiN gate) with a FlexDym 4 x 1 micro-well overlay that partitions the membrane into four chemically independent regions (approximately 2,176 pixels each, square-root-of-N averaging). Two wells carry capture antibodies (anti-IL-6, anti-IL-10), one is a non-specific reference, and one tests specificity; the transduced signal is defined as the differential current relative to the reference signal (Delta I_D(W_n) - Delta I_D(W_3)). Single-analyte dose-response measurements spanning 100 fM to 10 nM successfully resolve both IL-6 and IL-10 above the non-specific detection floor, including at healthy-serum baseline concentrations. The array shows a per-pixel pH sensitivity of 1.13 microamperes per pH unit (CV approximately 14%). Across two chips, device-to-device variation is dominated by transconductance spread (g_m CV approximately 62%); a one-time per-device g_m calibration reduces analyte-measurement variance to approximately 16%. We further validate the surface functionalization, characterize device-to-device variation, and demonstrate the FlexDym integration workflow. Simultaneous multiplexed cytokine measurements resolve IL-6 (W1) and IL-10 (W2) against the chemistry-only reference (W3). At the same time, cross-specificity characterization is assessed by applying IL-6 to an anti-IL-10 well (W4), establishing a scalable label-free ISFET architecture for multiplexed cytokine sensing.

items.abstract_text: RTL repair benchmarks should measure whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. To this end, we construct and hash-bind RTLRepairDataset, 5,784 (broken, fixed) training pairs; RTLRepairBench, 459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations; and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. We then use this infrastructure to identify two measurement confounds. First, simulation and formal scoring give opposite signs for the apparent effect of providing a specification in one evaluated cohort; reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics. Second, on 274 mined model failures, the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery point estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. Thus, a conventional repair score need not isolate whether the model used the faulty RTL. We translate these findings into evaluation controls: report initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics; disclose oracle coverage and undecided cases; and include a specification-only baseline. Together, the resources and audit provide both a benchmark for behavioral repair and a protocol for diagnosing what contributes to its measured score. We release the benchmark, the training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials at https://github.com/Evaaaz/RTLRepairBench.

items.title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
items.venue_name: arXiv
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables adaptive and autonomous decision-making in embedded, edge, and heterogeneous computing systems. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer low latency, energy efficiency, and architectural flexibility for RL deployment, while introducing challenges in resource constraints, implementation complexity, and hardware-algorithm co-design. This review surveys more than 100 studies on RL implementations across FPGA and IC platforms, emphasizing architectures, implementation strategies, performance evaluation, and applications. The literature is organized by RL family, including model-based Markov decision processes, classical value-based methods, deep RL, actor-critic, policy-gradient, and multi-agent approaches. We further classify studies by abstraction level, hardware realization strategy, and application domain, examining how RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware. Unlike surveys restricted to particular algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified analysis of FPGA and IC implementations, covering acceleration, reconfigurable architectures, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization.
items.abstract_text: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables adaptive and autonomous decision-making in embedded, edge, and heterogeneous computing systems. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer low latency, energy efficiency, and architectural flexibility for RL deployment, while introducing challenges in resource constraints, implementation complexity, and hardware-algorithm co-design. This review surveys more than 100 studies on RL implementations across FPGA and IC platforms, emphasizing architectures, implementation strategies, performance evaluation, and applications. The literature is organized by RL family, including model-based Markov decision processes, classical value-based methods, deep RL, actor-critic, policy-gradient, and multi-agent approaches. We further classify studies by abstraction level, hardware realization strategy, and application domain, examining how RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware. Unlike surveys restricted to particular algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified analysis of FPGA and IC implementations, covering acceleration, reconfigurable architectures, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Comparative assessments consider resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and reported performance gains. Finally, we identify recurring architectural patterns, practical limitations, open challenges, and research directions for efficient RL-driven hardware systems. The survey offers a consolidated reference for researchers developing and evaluating RL solutions on specialized hardware.
