items.abstract_text: Accurate IR drop analysis in 3D integrated circuits (3D ICs) is critical for ensuring power integrity and physical design convergence. However, conventional IR drop simulation flows suffer from extensive runtime and complicated flows, making them difficult for early-stage design evaluation and large-scale design iterations. To address this challenge, we propose DIONet3D, a novel dual-input dual-output neural network tailored for IR drop prediction in 3D ICs. DIONet3D takes feature maps from both top and bottom dies as input, incorporates a shared backbone with U-Net structure, and outputs IR drop maps for both dies simultaneously. To enhance the modeling of 3D power-delivery effects, we introduce a physics-guided 3D-Enhanced PDN representation, in which planar PDN stripes are converted into spatially continuous features through Gaussian kernel-based smoothing, while vertical HB/TSV connections are encoded to capture cross-die power delivery. This hybrid representation enables the network to capture both inter die and intra die features effectively while balancing the computation efficiency and feature representation efficiency. Furthermore, a compound loss function is proposed, combining multiple loss functions with dynamic weighting to balance multi-task convergence and improve structural consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art convolutional neural network (CNN) methods and achieves good generalization performance. Compared to commercial EDA simulation tools, DIONet3D achieves high structural and spatial similarity, with up to 309× runtime speedup and 89× memory reduction under CPU inference. Our results demonstrate that DIONet3D offers an accurate and lightweight surrogate solution for 3D IC IR drop evaluation.

items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) have emerged as a promising solution for 3-D spatial modeling, scene reconstruction, and AR/VR applications. However, NeRF rendering involves frequent and irregular off-chip memory accesses, particularly during ray sampling and hash encoding stages. Although existing edge platforms offer sufficient computational capability and memory bandwidth, such irregular memory access patterns lead to inefficient hardware utilization and significant latency overheads, making real-time rendering challenging. items.abstract_text: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) have emerged as a promising solution for 3-D spatial modeling, scene reconstruction, and AR/VR applications. However, NeRF rendering involves frequent and irregular off-chip memory accesses, particularly during ray sampling and hash encoding stages. Although existing edge platforms offer sufficient computational capability and memory bandwidth, such irregular memory access patterns lead to inefficient hardware utilization and significant latency overheads, making real-time rendering challenging. To address these issues, we present NeMO, an end-to-end accelerator specifically designed to enhance memory access efficiency in instant 3D rendering. NeMO incorporates three key innovations: 1) a novel occupancy grid compaction technique that completely eliminates off-chip memory accesses during the ray marching phase; 2) a hierarchical subgrid hashing strategy with block-by-block ray processing to optimize hash table access patterns, combined with a two-level cache architecture that reduces off-chip memory access by over 99% during multiresolution hash encoding; and 3) an end-to-end processor tailored for the NeRF pipeline, featuring fine-grained pipelining for ray marching and backpressure-enabled pipelining for multiresolution hash encoding. Implemented in a commercial 28-nm process technology, NeMO achieves real-time rendering at 79.23 FPS on synthetic datasets. It outperforms the Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin and high-end RTX 4080 graphics processing unit (GPU) by$51.78\times $and$6.43\times $in speed and$1767.08\times $and$493.17\times $in energy efficiency (EE), respectively. In addition, NeMO surpasses the latest NeRF accelerator, delivering$2.64\times $higher speed and a$28.7\times $off-chip bandwidth reduction, with per-frame memory access under 30 MB.

items.abstract_text: Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) play a crucial role in Electronic Design Automation (EDA) applications, which have been widely used in safety-critical environments, including aerospace, chip manufacturing, and medical devices. A critical stage in FPGA development is logic synthesis, which enables developers to translate their software designs into hardware net lists. However, bugs in FPGA logic synthesis compilers may lead to unexpected behaviors in target hardware net lists, which may cause potential security risks. Therefore, it is critical to detect and repair such bugs in FPGA logic synthesis compilers. While recent testing methods have made progress in automatic bug detection, they remain limited by a fundamental weakness, the generated test cases exhibit minimal timing complexity and structural diversity. To address this challenge, we propose a mutation-based method integrated with Bayesian optimization to detect bugs in FPGA logic synthesis compilers. The method, called SmootHDL, consists with three key components, the Test-program Generation Component (TPG), the Bayesian Diversity Selection Component (BDS), and the Equivalent Test Check Component (ETC). SmootHDL starts with a set of test cases which are called original test cases. To expand the timing test space, the TPG use a control-flow mutation strategy to generate new test cases which is functional equivalent with the original test cases. Furthermore, for increasing diversity of the generated test cases, the BDS combine the Bayesian optimizer to construct a selector based on the control-flow diversity. Finally, the ETC identifies bugs by comparing simulation outputs between original and generated test cases. Since the mutations preserve functional equivalence, functional equivalent test case should have same output. When SmootHDL detects any discrepancy between the outputs, it indicates a potential compiler bug. SmootHDL then reproduces the inconsistent behavior and reports the bug to official developers. We evaluated our method on the mainstream FPGA logic synthesis compilers. Experiments show that SmootHDL can generate more diverse test cases and detect more bugs compared with the latest testing methods for FPGA logic synthesis compilers. Over three months, SmootHDL found 16 bugs, 12 of which were confirmed by official technical support, and 6 have already been fixed.

items.title: Optimizing Unitary Coupled Cluster With Single and Double Kernels for Modern NISQ Architectures
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: The Unitary Coupled Cluster with Singles and Doubles (UCCSD) ansatz is a widely used kernel in quantum chemistry and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithms, but its execution on near-term superconducting quantum processors is hindered by high gate costs and limited qubit connectivity. Existing compilation approaches either adopt simultaneous synthesis, which efficiently diagonalizes excitations but ignores connectivity, or individual synthesis, which enforces connectivity-awareness but sacrifices optimization opportunities. In this work, we propose a connectivity-aware compiler framework for UCCSD kernels that combines the efficiency of simultaneous synthesis with the practicality of connectivity constraints. First, we introduce blockwise qubit mapping, which groups program qubits into excitation-specific blocks and maps them to internally connected regions of the hardware graph. Second, we design connectivity-aware synthesis rules that diagonalize excitations directly on the mapped hardware graph, reducing the number of SWAP gates. We implement our framework and evaluate it on molecular and random UCCSD kernels using Google Sycamore’s and IBMQ Manhattan’s connectivity. C
items.abstract_text: The Unitary Coupled Cluster with Singles and Doubles (UCCSD) ansatz is a widely used kernel in quantum chemistry and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithms, but its execution on near-term superconducting quantum processors is hindered by high gate costs and limited qubit connectivity. Existing compilation approaches either adopt simultaneous synthesis, which efficiently diagonalizes excitations but ignores connectivity, or individual synthesis, which enforces connectivity-awareness but sacrifices optimization opportunities. In this work, we propose a connectivity-aware compiler framework for UCCSD kernels that combines the efficiency of simultaneous synthesis with the practicality of connectivity constraints. First, we introduce blockwise qubit mapping, which groups program qubits into excitation-specific blocks and maps them to internally connected regions of the hardware graph. Second, we design connectivity-aware synthesis rules that diagonalize excitations directly on the mapped hardware graph, reducing the number of SWAP gates. We implement our framework and evaluate it on molecular and random UCCSD kernels using Google Sycamore’s and IBMQ Manhattan’s connectivity. Compared with state-of-the-art compilers, our approach reduces CNOT count by up to 34% and circuit depth by 49%, while improving VQE accuracy under noise.

items.title: Ising Placer: A Novel Framework for Placement Based on Ising Machine With Error-Correcting Multistage Annealing
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: As conventional placement algorithms face growing challenges, Ising machines offer a promising path for accelerating electronic design automation (EDA). This brief proposes a novel Ising model-based placement framework utilizing a Sequence-Pair (SP) to spin-matrix mapping, a custom Hamiltonian for constraints and wirelength, and an Error-Correcting Flipping with Multi-Stage Annealing (ECF-MSA) mechanism to ensure solution validity. Validated on an Ising machine simulator, our framework, when compared to state-of-the-art commercial and academic PCB placement tools, reduces routed wirelength by 8-18% with an estimated 37x to over 431x speedup on future hardware. This work demonstrates the significant potential of physics-based computing for complex EDA problems.

Transitioning from binary to ternary computation offers substantial improvements in energy efficiency. This paper proposes a novel ternary full adder (TFA) architecture implemented with 42 transistors using multi-threshold carbon nanotube FET (CNTFET) technology. Circuit-level simulations performed in Synopsys HSPICE at 0.9 V demonstrate that the proposed TFA achieves a reduction of 35.8%–75.2% in power consumption and 21.6%–70% in energy consumption compared to state-of-the-art designs. Reliability analysis, based on extensive Monte Carlo simulations, confirms that the proposed architecture exhibits the lowest sensitivity to variations in key CNTFET process parameters. These advantages come at the expense of a moderate delay overhead and a 1.85× increase in layout area relative to a highly compact design. To further validate its practical impact, the TFA is evaluated in an image-processing application leveraging ternary logic based on a hardware algorithm. The results indicate up to 38.86% energy savings while preserving accuracy and output quality. Additionally, a comprehensive benchmarking framework is introduced, combining hardware efficiency and quality metrics into a unified figure of merit (FoM). Under this FoM, the proposed design outperforms the best existing counterpart by approximately 76.21%. The demonstrated trade-off between energy efficiency and accuracy highlights the proposed CNTFET-based TFA as a promising candidate for the design of future high-performance and energy-aware ternary computing systems.

items.abstract_text: Curvilinear masks play a crucial role in maintaining the lithographic fidelity for advanced nodes, but severe mask rule check (MRC) violations frequently emerge in conventional variable-shaped beam (VSB) mask data preparation (MDP) workflows. These conventional workflows rely on shape-based or dose-based mask process correction (MPC) prior to shot fracturing. Shape-based MPC methods rely on the movement of manually designed segmented lines for edge displacement corrections, which fail for complex curvilinear designs with dense line segments of arbitrary directions. While dose-based approaches handle curvilinear geometries, they are computationally intensive and incompatible with most VSB mask writers. Worse, subsequent fracturing often compromises the MPCed mask to enhance manufacturability, degrading mask quality. In this work, we propose Shot Splatting, an innovative MPC framework that integrates traditional MPC and shot fracturing into a unified optimization process, achieving end-to-end MDP processing. By optimizing shot fracturing strategies in conjunction with geometry, placement, size, and dose, our method achieves 22.3% EPE reduction and 7.87% fewer shots without introducing extra MRC violations, at a moderate computational cost of 5.01s compared to 3s for the state-of-the-art method. The output of our framework, i.e., optimized shots, can be directly formatted for VSB writers, enabling seamless fabrication.

Similarly, the D flip-flop exhibits a 36.46% to 52.34% reduction in cell count, 30.77% to 67.86% in area, 40.00% to 76.92% in delay, 77.27% to 98.31% in cost, and 46.48% to 62.47% in power consumption. items.abstract_text: Circuit pipelining is essential for improving the frequency and throughput of sequential circuits, yet it still largely relies on manual design at the behavioral level, which is effort-intensive, error-prone, and fails to exploit fine-grained gate-level opportunities. Existing automatic approaches analyze feedforward paths to insert registers but fall back to conservative stalling in the presence of feedback loops, sacrificing parallelism to preserve correctness. As a result, neither manual nor existing automatic methods simultaneously achieve fine-grained throughput optimization and correctness guarantees on arbitrary sequential circuits. We present an automatic pipelining framework that combines gate-level forwarding and customized scheduling. Our key insight is that gate-level analysis reveals shorter feedback loops, whose hazards can be resolved by forwarding paths spanning fewer pipeline stages, thus avoiding long multi-cycle dependencies that cause redundant stalls. Our method consists of two steps: the first focuses on fine-grained optimization beyond behavioral-level analysis, while the second ensures correctness for arbitrary circuits. Concretely, we (i) greedily assign pipeline stages at the gate level and create short forwarding paths for fine-grained pipeline optimization, and (ii) design a circuit-specific scheduler to ensure correctness. The scheduler analyzes state-conditioned reads/writes to predict future dependencies and apply only the necessary stalls, and is then synthesized into hardware using an improved Binary Speculative Diagram (BSD) algorithm with acceptable hardware overhead. Across diverse circuit datasets, our approach identifies 35.23% redundant pipeline stalls overlooked by behavioral-level manual designs and improves throughput by 9.46% for 3-stage and 23.07% for 4-stage pipelines over EDA-based automatic pipelining techniques, while guaranteeing functional correctness on arbitrary sequential circuits.

items.abstract_text: Recently, machine learning-based techniques have been increasingly employed for layout hotspot detection. However, existing supervised-based methods often struggle to learn a reliable decision boundary across the entire dataset and ignore the geometric properties and topology of the polygons. Moreover, robustness to geometric transformations of layout patterns has received limited attention in hotspot detection, potentially affecting model generalization. To address these challenges, this article introduces GRC-HD, a novel contrastive learning framework that aligns image features with layout topology representations while integrating geometric-robust feature learning. The framework improves the ability to distinguish between hotspots and non-hotspots by similarity computations instead of a single decision boundary. To effectively incorporate geometric information into the model training process, we propose Layout2Seq, which encodes polygon shapes as vector sequences and feeds them into GRC-HD. Furthermore, to better represent topological information, we develop an absolute position embedding, replacing the standard position encoders used in Transformer architectures. To improve the robustness of hotspot detector, we design a configurable geometric transformation library that generates multiple manufacturing-relevant views. The library is leveraged through an auxiliary Siamese network during training for geometric-robust representation learning, and through a self-calibration voting strategy at inference, where transformed instances act as independent voters to enhance decision reliability. Extensive experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate that GRC-HD outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

items.abstract_text: ZNS SSDs are increasingly adopted in data centers, leveraging fixed-size zones with coarse-grained mapping and sequential write constraints to mitigate over-provisioning and write amplification. When a zone is exclusively used by a workload, sending sequential read/write transactions together to the backend can leverage plane-level parallelism within the zone. However, when multiple workloads share the same ZNS SSD—even accessing distinct zones—they still compete for back-end physical resources, which we refer to as zone interaction. We observe that current transaction scheduling strategies for ZNS SSDs do not fully consider the impact of zone interaction between workloads, which leads to reduced fairness and QoS degradation. First, chip-level queues are scheduled independently, considering only intra-queue zone interactions. This can cause transaction adjustment to expand global unfairness across workloads. Second, fairness-oriented scheduling methods interleave transactions from different workloads (zones), which prevents ZNS sequential write requests that could exploit plane-level parallelism from being issued to the backend storage simultaneously. To address these challenges, we propose FANS, a fairness scheduler for shared ZNS SSDs. FANS globally perceives the impact of zone interactions across different workloads and achieves global fairness through a two-phase transaction adjustment strategy. Within each workqueue, FANS employs zone-aware scheduling to ensure that plane-level parallelism can be fully utilized. Evaluations with mixed workloads show FANS achieves 22% higher fairness and 62% greater throughput compared to state-of-the-art frameworks.

items.title: Optimizing High-Level Synthesis Sparse Matrix--Vector Kernel for Alveo FPGAs
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is a critical kernel in scientific computing and high-performance applications, yet it remains challenging to optimize due to irregular memory access patterns and low computational intensity. This work targets the AMD Vitis SpMV kernel on HBM-equipped Alveo FPGAs and introduces hardware-aware optimizations that significantly improve performance, especially in reduced precision scenarios. Building on prior evaluations of the Vitis kernel, we propose two key enhancements: coefficient grouping and index packet coalescing. These reduce padding overhead and improve memory bandwidth efficiency without requiring a complete redesign of the vendor-supplied kernel. Experimental results over 33 matrices from the SuiteSparse collection show up to 4× speedup and an average improvement of 1.6× compared to the original Vitis kernel. Our method demonstrates how practical architectural adaptations can yield substantial performance gains, supporting the growing trend toward lower-precision and energy-efficient computing in FPGA-based accelerators.

items.abstract_text: IoT sensors and devices heavily rely on cloud-based processing, especially in healthcare monitoring, for sensor data analysis, which incurs high data transfer costs and energy consumption. To reduce constant data transmission, always-on smart sensors can use lightweight brain-inspired Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models to efficiently classify sensor data that require further resource-intensive cloud processing. The proposed architecture maintains HDC algorithm accuracy with 8-bit integer precision for complex datasets, where 1-bit quantization is not feasible. We propose SenseHD, an all-digital CMOS always-on smart sensor accelerator for energy-constrained smart sensing applications. SenseHD achieves an extremely small power consumption of 39.21 - 92.59 μWdepending on design parameterization, supporting 8-bit hypervectors and an energy-efficient near-memory fused item memory + multiply-accumulate systolic array encoder. We introduce a novel systolic similarity search unit that utilizes a small systolic array to calculate hypervector cosine similarity metrics, consuming only 110.89 nJ/inference. By intelligently transmitting only relevant data, SenseHD reduces system-level energy consumption by up to 8.8× compared to a cloud-centric baseline. Notably, the accelerator overhead is negligible, consuming only 1.2% of the total system energy.

State-of-the-art GHR attacks can successfully extract bits stored in the GHR, inferring branch directions of executed conditional branch instructions, with conditions linked to secrets. However, retrieving GHR bits requires knowledge of the victim’s virtual address layout. GHLeaker retrieves GHR branch information by correlating different branches, effectively bypassing kernel address isolation. items.abstract_text: The Global History Register (GHR), an essential component of the Conditional Branch Predictor (CBP) in modern processors, has become a popular attack target because it stores recent branch histories including sensitive kernel control flow information. State-of-the-art GHR attacks can successfully extract bits stored in the GHR, inferring branch directions of executed conditional branch instructions, with conditions linked to secrets. However, retrieving GHR bits requires knowledge of the victim’s virtual address layout. Advancements in enhanced kernel address isolation techniques have significantly reduced the risk of these GHR attacks. In this paper, we introduce GHLeaker, a novel control-flow-based side-channel attack (SCA) that does not rely on kernel address knowledge. GHLeaker retrieves GHR branch information by correlating different branches, effectively bypassing kernel address isolation. We applied GHLeaker to attack Intel, AMD, and ARM processors, demonstrating that all these mainstream processors are vulnerable to the attack. On these platforms, GHLeaker successfully extracts secrets from the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) and Montgomery ladder algorithm which is widely used in cryptography systems such as RSA.

items.title: SpikeLet: Empowering Multichiplet Neuromorphic System With Hierarchical Interconnect and Spatial–Temporal Parallelism
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: As Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) scale, their neuron counts exceed the capacity of a single chip, necessitating multi-chip integration. Multi-chiplet systems provide dense, high-bandwidth interconnects but suffer from inefficient inter-chip spike transmission, limited parallelism, and the lack of transmission-aware mapping. We present SpikeLet, the first multi-chiplet neuromorphic system tailored for large-scale SNNs. SpikeLet employs a hierarchical transmission interconnect with an extend-AER protocol to aggregate spikes and decouple intra- and inter-chiplet communication, an event-driven spatial–temporal parallel dataflow that enables cross-layer and cross-timestep parallelism, and a communication-aware hierarchical mapping based on cooperative co-evolution to balance computation and communication across chiplets and cores. On a 4×4-chiplet prototype, SpikeLet reduces transmission latency by 74.2%, improves throughput by 36.6×, and boosts energy efficiency by 39.2× over a 2D multi-chip baseline, demonstrating a compact and scalable platform for next-generation neuromorphic computing.

By combining the ideas of alternating direction implicit (ADI) method, recursive algorithm with the circuit topology of the array, this simulation method achieves precise modeling of the equivalent conductance matrix (input-output relationship) for the arrays containing interconnect resistance with a computational complexity of O(mn) (for anm×narray). The method not only guarantees theoretical convergence, but also demonstrates orders-of-magnitude speed improvement over existing solutions and commercial tool, requiring only 3.2 seconds to simulate 1M cell scale arrays. Leveraging this simulation approach, we determined the precise deployment scheme for a CNN model for on 1M memristor arrays within ten minutes, reducing the relative error between the array’s equivalent conductance matrices and target CNN weight matrices from ~50% to less than 1%. This effectively compensates for IR-drop effects, restoring the hardware’s inference accuracy from 57.3% to 96.9% - nearly matching ideal software models.

However, the embedding layers of DLRMs have emerged as a significant performance bottleneck due to their high demands on memory capacity and bandwidth. Existing solutions, such as offloading to CPU memory, are hampered by communication overheads, while many proposed Processing-In-Memory (PIM) architectures are not yet commercially viable, limiting their practical impact. A promising approach, demonstrated by recent work like UpDLRM, is to accelerate these layers using commercial Processing-In-Memory (PIM) hardware. However, this approach does not address the challenge of ever-growing model sizes in industrial-scale systems. To tackle both memory bandwidth and capacity limitations, this paper proposesGPAQuant, a framework that co-designs PIM-based acceleration with model quantization. GPAQuant strategically stores quantized embedding tables (EMTs) in distributed DPU memory and offloads both the memory-intensive lookups and reductions to the DPUs. To address DPU-specific challenges, we propose four key innovations: (1) architecture-aware EMT partitioning that optimizes data placement to minimize inter-DPU communication, (2) frequency-aware workload balancing to evenly distribute access patterns across DPUs, (3) fine-grained EMT rearrangement that reduces quantization errors while preserving spatial locality, and (4) group-wise quantization to balance dequantization overhead and model accuracy. Extensive evaluations across six datasets and four DLRM architectures demonstrate GPAQuant’s superiority: it achieves 4.6× speedup on embedding layers and 3.4× end-to-end inference acceleration compared to state-of-the-art CPU-GPU implementations and PIM baselines, with negligible accuracy loss.

items.abstract_text: Variations in the computational capabilities of edge devices and runtime resource availability pose considerable challenges in developing efficient ubiquitous inference. Dynamic Neural Networks (DyNNs) have been developed to address device heterogeneity by adapting network structures or parameters to complex deployment environments. However, existing DyNN methods are largely insensitive to runtime resource variations and hardware-specific configurations, and their reliance on extensive profiling complicates deployment. In this work, we present Cheerful, a hardware-oriented, ubiquitous early exit framework that enables efficient inference on heterogeneous devices by combining hardware-parameterized performance modeling and optimization with online adaptation to resource variations. In the offline stage, Cheerful models key performance metrics by integrating comprehensive analytical and data-driven methods, formulates an optimization problem to achieve the trade-off between inference accuracy and energy cost, and incorporates hardware-specific parameters to accommodate device heterogeneity. In the online stage, Cheerful integrates a lightweight hardware-aware inference engine (HIE) that jointly adjusts early-exit configurations and CPU frequency based on run-time resource availability, using Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS). Extensive experiments on heterogeneous devices demonstrate that Cheerful outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the accuracy-energy Pareto frontier in resource-constrained environments while maintaining low deployment overhead.

The existing nonlinear placers provide higher computational efficiency than heuristic algorithms, but their insufficient attention to the initialization of GP distributions limits rapid convergence towards high-quality global optimal solutions. To resolve this, we propose a GP framework, DrlGoFPGA 2.0, combining LUT, FF, DSP, and RAM (LFDR) instance placement generation based on multi-agent graph transformer network (MAGTN) and LFDR initial placement fine-tuning based on nonlinear placement. A MAGTN model for LFDR initial placement is designed, which utilizes distributed training to circumvent the issues of sub-optimal placement models and prolonged training times due to the non-uniform distribution of large-scale LFDR sites. A lightweight LFDR line-network relationships (LNR) graph supporting MAGTN co-decision is created by separating, renumbering, and deduplicating the LNR graph containing all instances, and inputting the LFDR LNR graph into MAGTN to obtain the connections between LFDRs. The experimental results on ISPD’2016/2017 benchmarks show that compared with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) nonlinear placer, DrlGoFPGA 2.0 can improve GP speed by 27.3% ∼ 82.1%, reduce half-perimeter wirelength by 0.6% ∼ 4.6%, and routed wirelength by 0.4% ∼ 2.8%.

items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: In this paper, we introduce LIMCA, a novelfine-tuning-freeLarge Language Model (LLM)-driven framework for automating the design and evaluation of In-Memory Computing (IMC) crossbar architectures. Unlike traditional approaches, where the manual, knowledge-intensive design process and the lack of high-quality circuit netlists have significantly constrained Design Space Exploration (DSE) and optimization to behavioral system-level tools, LIMCA employs a No-Human-In-Loop (NHIL) automated pipeline to generate and validate circuit netlists for SPICE simulations, eliminating manual intervention. LIMCA systematically explores the IMC design space by leveraging a structured dataset and LLM-based performance evaluation. Our experimental results on MNIST classification demonstrate that LIMCA successfully generates crossbar designs achieving ≥96% accuracy while maintaining a power consumption ≤3W, making this the first work in LLM-assisted IMC DSE. Compared to existing frameworks, LIMCA provides an automated, scalable, and hardware-aware solution, reducing design exploration time while ensuring user-constrained performance trade-offs. Artifacts are open-sourced at https://github.com/ACADLab/LI

items.title: Juggler: A Dynamic Warp Scheduler for GPGPUs
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: General-Purpose Graphics Processing Units (GPGPUs) accelerate various applications, ranging from graphics rendering to scientific simulations and machine learning (ML). The warp scheduler is a critical element in GPGPUs. It needs to manage thread execution in a way that optimizes performance as well as efficiency. However, different applications, and even different phases of the same application, have varying performance requirements. Hence, fixed static scheduling algorithms are suboptimal. This brief introduces a dynamic warp scheduler namedJuggler, which dynamically switches between different scheduling strategies at runtime based on phase-specific performance characteristics. Juggler predicts and switches to the most suitable scheduling mode at runtime while improving the overall performance. Evaluations demonstrate that Juggler improves performance by up to 24.84%, with an average gain of 4.66% over state-of-the-art schedulers. These results emphasize the capability of dynamic scheduling to unlock even greater computational power of the GPGPUs.

items.abstract_text: Side-channel attacks pose a critical threat to cryptographic devices, with horizontal attacks being a primary strategy when the secret information is changed in each execution. The modular multiplication is a frequent target of horizontal attacks, which can pose a threat to the secret such as BRIP algorithm. In our research, we found that existing leakage assessment frameworks often perform poorly for modular multiplications in a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) environment. Our analysis reveals that the leakage magnitude and position are greatly influenced by shared operands, specifically the Hamming distance between corresponding segments processed by the multiplier units. This dependency fundamentally limits traditional approaches. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel collision leakage model centered at the multiplier-unit level. The operand-dependent model demonstrates the impact of shared operands on leakage in modular multiplication. Building upon this model, we propose a refined leakage assessment framework that integrates clustering algorithms, the TVLA methodology, and adaptive threshold setting. This framework possesses trace filtering capabilities, dynamically identifying traces with sufficient leakage. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, we design and conduct a horizontal clustering attack on BRIP algorithm in an ECDSA implementations. The results show that traces passing our framework’s filter achieve a high secret scalar recovery success rate. Furthermore, comparative analysis confirms that our framework offers significant advantages over traditional methods like PCA, covariance, and semi-parametric approaches, particularly in low-SNR condition.

items.title: Power Budgeting of Homogeneous 3-D Processors in Dark Silicon
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: The performance of 3-D processors is constrained by the power budget, defined as the maximum power consumption to guarantee the system’s thermal safety. In this work, we present a dynamic power budgeting method for homogeneous 3-D processors in dark silicon. The new method provides a power budget that leads to higher system potential performance over the existing methods with two new techniques. First, a sub-optimal active core distribution in 3-D space is computed on the fly which increases the total power budget. Second, we introduce an intelligent power assignment strategy across die layers with optimal power ratios computed offline, which further increases the potential system performance. Experiments on two homogeneous 3-D processors with different architectures show that the new method leads to a higher system performance, compared with the existing techniques.

items.abstract_text: Edge–cloud collaborative video analytics has become essential for intelligent monitoring and semantic segmentation in large-scale IoT systems. However, existing approaches cannot efficiently adapt to new and dynamic environments and often rely on heavy edge-side neural inference, causing high latency and resource waste. In this paper, we propose LEAF, a Lightweight Edge–cloud Analysis Filtering framework for low-latency semantic segmentation. LEAF employs a compressed-domain multi-cue strategy that leverages motion vectors, residuals, andUchannel differences to detect scene changes. Unchanged regions are reused while only updated regions are re-inferred, reducing redundant edge computation and uplink transmission. To improve robustness in dynamic scenes, we introduce a stabilization mechanism for fusion weight prediction. By modeling periodic patterns and observation cues, the mechanism produces smooth and reliable weight estimates, enhancing temporal stability and mitigating cold-start instability. Furthermore, we design a periodic edge– cloud prediction–update protocol. The edge performs lightweight per-frame detection and weight prediction, while the cloud periodically conducts full-frame segmentation to update filtering parameters and returns compact updates. This closed-loop update mechanism maintains long-term accuracy under limited bandwidth. Extensive experiments on real-world driving and traffic monitoring datasets demonstrate that LEAF reduces end-to-end per-frame latency by up to 2× while lowering bandwidth usage and edge computational load. LEAF maintains comparable task accuracy and exhibits stable performance across different scenarios, enabling low-latency and resource-efficient semantic segmentation in dynamic edge–cloud environments.

items.title: Behavioral Modeling of RF-Input DLMBA Based on Optimized DVR Model Using Improved PSO Algorithm
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: This work presents a behavioral modeling methodology for a recently reported multi-transistor power amplifier (PA) utilizing a novel architecture, as RF-Input divisional load-modulated balanced amplifier (RF-Input DLMBA). Due to the active nonlinear load modulation between multiple active devices, this type of PA exhibits significant nonlinearity as well as memory effects that are difficult to model using traditional techniques. An improved particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm with dynamic nonlinear self-adaptive hyperparameters (PSO-DNSH) has been employed for the threshold optimization of the decomposed vector rotation (DVR) model in this work. An introduction to the basic principles and modeling procedures of this proposed technique is provided. RF-input DLMBAs, which are designed in-house, have been used for modeling and digital predistortion (DPD) validation for different output powers, signal bandwidths, and back-off ranges. The results indicate that, as compared with traditional models and standard PSO-based DVR models, better prediction performance has been achieved by the proposed model.

items.summary: With increasing integration density, modern Systems-on-Chips (SoCs), especially on-chip caches and memories, are critically vulnerable to soft errors. Error Correcting Codes (ECC) are the most widely adopted mitigation technique in safety-critical SoCs, making accurate modeling of ECC overheads essential for effective design decisions. Existing cache modeling frameworks such as CACTI consider only the memory overheads for storing ECC check-bits, and neglect the delay and energy costs of ECC combinational logic, assuming them negligible. We extend CACTI to include the delay and energy overheads due to the ECC logic along with the memory-induced ECC overheads. In addition to the configurations supported by CACTI, we model High Reliability (HR) and High Performance (HP) modes of ECC operation for flexible design exploration. Extensive evaluation across SPEC CPU 2006 and MiBench workloads demonstrates the effectiveness of our modeling, highlighting that neglecting logic overheads underestimates the ECC performance and energy overheads by 12% and 18%, respectively, for SPEC CPU 2006, and 12% and 17%, respectively, for MiBench.

items.title: A High-Accuracy, Hybrid Scalable Model for MIM Capacitors Over Wide Temperature for MMIC Applications
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: Conventional Process Design Kits for Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits (MMICs) often lack capacitor models that are robust across wide temperature and frequency ranges, posing a significant challenge to the design reliability and first-pass success. To address this, a novel π-type equivalent circuit with grounding inductors is developed, yielding S-parameter fitting errors under 2% while also explaining the device’s thermal resonant drift. Building on this, a hybrid scalable model synergizing a physics-guided core with neural network compensation is proposed. This methodology demonstrates exceptional accuracy, achieving parameter-fitting R-squared values above 0.999. More importantly, the final model’s S-parameter predictions maintain an R-squared greater than 0.98 against measured data across the entire temperature and geometry space. This work provides a highly accurate, scalable MIM capacitor model essential for robust circuit design under harsh operating conditions and offers a generalizable hybrid methodology applicable to other passive components, enhancing the predictive power of modern PDKs.

items.abstract_text: The commercialization of Resistive Random Access Memories (RRAMs) has been invested by many companies as an alternative to conventional memories. This necessitates a thorough comprehension of manufacturing defects to create high-quality, efficient test and diagnosis solutions that will facilitate high-volume production. This work presents the identification and characterization of a novel defect, called Ion Depletion (ID), utilising silicon measurements. In the selected defective device, after excluding the first 100 unstable cycles, 14% of the remaining 836 cycles exhibit ID-defective High Resistance State (HRS) degradation, while the low resistance state remains unaffected. Furthermore, this unique defect is non-linear and inside the device itself; hence, the conventional defect and fault modeling, which relies on linear resistors beside the device, cannot be applied to model the ID defect. To tackle this issue, the Device-Aware (DA) defect modeling approach is used. A calibrated RRAM model representing the defective device is developed using measurement data to precisely characterize how the defect influences the electrical properties of the memory hardware. Subsequently, fault analysis is conducted based on the DA defect model, leading to the introduction of suitable fault models. These models demonstrate that the ID defect can trigger undefined state faults. Finally, dedicated test and diagnosis solutions specifically designed for the ID defect are proposed.

items.abstract_text: For precision motion control systems, real-time feedforward compensation is indispensable, yet its implementation is constrained by latency, computational/storage hardware resources. Classic approaches, including online model-based feedforward and iterative learning control feedforward, fail to balance accuracy and generalization. Although offline neural network feedforward (NN-FF) has emerged as a potent alternative, in-depth investigation into its real-time deployment is still lacking. Furthermore, even state-of-the-art, offline recurrent NN-FF (RNN-FF) models impose substantial demands on hardware resources (due to large parameters and inherent sequential processing), making them less suitable for efficient real-time implementation. This paper proposes a generalized hardware-model co-optimization framework for real-time NN-FF. Specifically, we develop Motion Residual Convolution (MRC): a compact CNN-based model with high accuracy, strong generalization, lightweight design, and inherent parallelism for latency reduction. Correspondingly, we construct an accelerator core with 10 vector multiply-accumulate (VMAC) units for multi-filter parallel processing. For two scenarios with distinct priorities, specifically the resource-constrained and the latency-constrained, we adopt spatial feedforward acceleration engine (SFAE) and temporal feedforward acceleration engine (TFAE), respectively. SFAE maximizes throughput via independent VMAC arrays per convolutional layer, while TFAE optimizes resource utilization through time-multiplexing a single VMAC array across layers. Experiments indicate MRC outperforms RNN-based counterparts in accuracy, using <1% of their storage and computational resources. The proposed accelerators achieve high energy efficiency with compact hardware resources, benefiting from the lightweight MRC model. Moreover, both accelerators achieve effective trade-offs: compared with TFAE, SFAE consumes 6.9–40.9% more key logic resources and 3.1% more power but delivers an average 61× execution speedup, achieving an energy efficiency of 222.2 GOPS/W.

items.abstract_text: The placement of Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) plays a critical role in modern electronic system design. In contrast to integrated circuit placement, which has been largely automated through advanced algorithms, PCB placement still relies heavily on manual efforts. This is primarily due to the restrictive constraints that devices with vastly different sizes and irregular shapes must be placed within extremely high-density, high-granularity, and limited spaces in the placement process of modern PCBs. Moreover, routing constraints such as the routability of surface-layer traces must be taken into account. These challenges have significantly hindered the advancement of fully automated industrial PCB placement algorithms for many years. To address the challenges, we propose ISPCBPlace, a gradient-based placement method for modern irregular-shaped PCBs under complex design constraints. We formulate the PCB global placement problem as a gradient-based optimization task and propose three key gradient formulation, boundary gradient, overlap gradient (incorporating a centrifugal gradient), and half-perimeter wire-length gradient, to enable effective convergence while satisfying design constraints. Furthermore, we propose a module-aware clustering method to enhance routability of surface-layer traces, and introduce a simulated annealing-based fine-tuning strategy to optimize component orientations and ensure legalization. Experimental results within real-world industrial PCB cases demonstrate that ISPCBPlace outperforms the state-of-the-art methods and even manual designs in terms of wire length, and successfully meeting industrial constraints.

items.abstract_text: Floorplanning is a critical phase in VLSI physical design, focusing on determining block positions while optimizing wirelength under specified area constraints. However, classical analytical-based floorplanners are highly sensitive to the quality of initial solutions, and existing learning-based methods often suffer from high computational inefficiency and complexity. In this paper, we propose a customized diffusion model to directly generate high-quality initial floorplans. By leveraging a classical analytical-based floorplanner on top of this initial floorplan, the final floorplanning results are significantly improved. To enhance feature extraction, a heterogeneous graph neural network (HGNN) is developed to explicitly incorporate block-to-block and pin-to-block relationships from the netlist during the diffusion process. We further propose a classifier-free conditional diffusion method based on adaptive maximum-mean discrepancy (Ada-MMD) to guide the generation process without relying on external classifiers. The Ada-MMD mechanism adaptively captures structural correlations in the latent space, improving conditional consistency and enabling more controllable and accurate initial floorplan generation. Additionally, a novel guidance sampling function is introduced to optimize both wirelength and overlap, effectively reducing the required sampling steps while maintaining competitive initial solutions. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating our proposed diffusion model with an advanced analytical-based floorplanner achieves at least 10.8% reduction in runtime and 3.8% reduction in HPWL compared to the original state-of-the-art floorplanner and other diffusion-based methods.

items.title: Designing Multiple Queues to Support Asynchronous Traffic Shaping in TSN Switches
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: Asynchronous Traffic Shaping (ATS) extends conventional synchronized Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) with an asynchronous scheduler to guarantee bounded end-to-end delay. Specifically, ATS introduces additional shaping queues prior to standard priority queues, eliminating the need for global clock synchronization and specific periodic traffic patterns. However, the current queue structure in TSN switches, inherited from Ethernet, does not support ATS. In this paper, we leverage the potential of virtual queues in the shared buffer switch to design multiple queues (MQ) that support ATS. The proposed design organizes queues as logical entities, with all queues sharing a common buffer space, achieving high resource utilization. We prototype MQ with ATS functionality on FPGA switches and evaluate its performance on hardware platforms. Experimental results show that our design introduces negligible additional end-to-end delay, maintains line-rate throughput, and incurs minimal resource overhead while satisfying the timing and shaping requirements defined by ATS.

items.abstract_text: The exponential growth of artificial intelligence (AI) applications has strained conventional von Neumann architectures, where frequent data transfers between compute units and memory create significant energy and latency bottlenecks. Compute-in-Memory (CIM) addresses this challenge by performing multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations directly in memory arrays, substantially reducing data movement. As transformers increasingly dominate AI workloads, extending CIM frameworks to support these architectures becomes critical. In this work, we present NeuroSim V1.5, an integrated framework for cooptimizing accuracy and hardware efficiency in CIM accelerator design. Key contributions include: (1) a hybrid ACIM/DCIM architecture enabling transformer acceleration, with a case study comparing vision transformer (ViT) and CNN performance; (2) an integrated co-optimization framework combining TensorRT-based quantization, flexible noise modeling, and circuit-level PPA estimation; (3) expanded device support including non-volatile capacitive memories; and (4) up to 6.5× faster runtime through GPU-accelerated simulation. Our ViT case study reveals that ViTs exhibit lower noise tolerance and area efficiency than CNNs of comparable size, suggesting CNNs remain well-suited for vision applications on CIM hardware. The hybrid architecture provides the foundation for future transformer workloads including large language models. All versions are available open-source at https://github.com/neurosim/NeuroSim.

This work focuses on enabling detailed power estimation for embedded processor cores within a core-based system-level design environment. Traditional RTL or gate-level simulation, while accurate, is too slow to support early system level decision making. To address this limitation, power modeling has emerged as a promising but challenging solution. The key innovation lies in using a minimal feature set mainly based on processor control signals, which significantly reduces modeling overhead. To ensure generality, we employ a residual-based model that combines linear regression and decision tree techniques to capture residual error information, making the model highly adaptive to unseen data. To obtain a power model, we explore the modeling space across various modeling alternatives, evaluating their performance in terms of accuracy and modeling effort. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves a cycle-by-cycle power prediction error of less than 3% and a simulation speed of 6.6Mcycles/s. The proposed methodology is integrated within an automated framework, streamlining both dataset generation and model training processes. This automation ensures efficiency and scalability, significantly reducing manual effort for the IP developer.

items.abstract_text: As superconducting quantum processors scale beyond thousands of qubits, manual layout methods pose the primary bottleneck to industrial deployment. Traditional quantum electronic design automation (EDA) tools emphasize component-level modeling but lack full-chip integration for scalable systems. This work formulates scalable superconducting quantum chip design as a geometric constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) and introduces GeoSynth, a constraint-aware automation framework to accelerate scalable quantum chip design. By leveraging global symmetry and local similarity of quantum chip, GeoSynth enables hierarchical constraint decomposition through four novel algorithms: adaptive launch pad allocation (GeoSynth-ALA), systematic component correspondence (GeoSynth-SCC), scalable template-based routing synthesis (GeoSynth-TRS), and global constraint propagation (GeoSynth-GCP). Implemented in EDA-Q, GeoSynth delivers an end-to-end automation flow for a 156-qubit flip-chip processor in 2,882 seconds. This represents a 2× speedup over a prior method that addressed only the routing subproblem for 64 qubits, and is crowned by the first fabrication validation of an automatically generated large-scale layout, achieving a T1 coherence time of 69.24 μs. Beyond fabrication validation, GeoSynth demonstrates robust scalability by successfully generating layouts for diverse configurations spanning 64 to 620 qubits across multiple architectural variants, confirming its capability to handle industrially relevant scales. GeoSynth’s efficient, constraint-driven automation offers a scalable solution for quantum hardware industrialization.

items.abstract_text: Owing to the inherent advantages of edge computing in latency, privacy, and always-on availability, Deep Neural Network (DNN) tasks are progressively shifting to edge devices. However, limited edge resources pose significant challenges for deploying large DNNs. Pipeline parallelism (PP) and post-training quantization (PTQ) are essential techniques for addressing these resource constraints, and mainstream frameworks (e.g., DeepSpeed, PyTorch) encapsulate them independently. Nonetheless, this decoupled treatment inevitably traps the optimization process into local optima and results in inferior throughput-accuracy trade-offs in heterogeneous edge environments, due to the natural circular dependency between the PP and PTQ optimization processes. To this end, we propose MP3, a novel framework for joint PP-PTQ optimization in heterogeneous edge environments. MP3 integrates three core components: (1) Task-Device Co-analyzer (TDC) utilizes a fine-grained modeling method to estimate computation and communication latencies precisely. (2) Information-Fused Accuracy Proxy (FAP) characterizes quantized DNN accuracy through a unified proxy combining intra-layer and inter-layer information, with a data-driven fusion function search strategy. (3) Pipeline Quantization Co-optimizer (PQC), leveraging latency estimates from TDC and accuracy characterizations from FAP, navigates the joint optimization space effectively by formulating it as a Constraint Programming (CP) problem. A comprehensive experimental evaluation on an edge testbed confirms the effectiveness of MP3, demonstrating that it lies on a superior Pareto curve (achieving up to 3.2× throughput speedup with accuracy drop within 1%) and exhibits robust adaptability across heterogeneous devices.

items.abstract_text: Dynamic Heterogeneous GNNs (DyHGNNs) are increasingly employed to model the complex relationships between various types of vertices and edges in real-world applications. When performing DyHGNN inference, existing software/hardware solutions adopt the snapshot-by-snapshot execution approach, and suffer from frequent and irregular access to identical neighbors for the same vertex across multiple snapshots, leading to redundant computations and irregular memory accesses. To address these challenges, we propose an efficient cross-snapshot hardware accelerator, i.e., COSH, which facilitates high-performance execution of DyHGNN inference. Specifically, we integrate a redundancy-aware asynchronous Filter-Load-Aggregate-Gather (FLAG) execution model into the accelerator design to minimize redundant computation and off-chip memory accesses. FLAG traverses the neighbors of the same vertex across different snapshots to identify all involved vertices and filter out changes in neighbors between consecutive snapshots. Then, it computes intermediate aggregation features for all encountered neighbors and incrementally calculates the results for the vertices in each snapshot, eliminating redundant computations and regularizing memory accesses. To minimize redundant accesses for vertex features, we also design a hierarchical data loading mechanism to provide a parallelized cross-snapshot filter to enhance the efficiency of processing graph structures. Besides, a coordinated feature aggregator is also proposed to synchronize feature aggregation and gathering, ensuring the timely utilization and management of generated intermediate features to boost computational parallelism. Our experimental results demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art software and hardware solutions, COSH achieves performance improvements of 27.1x and 3.6x on average, and also energy efficiency gains of 29.5x and 3.7x on average, respectively.

items.abstract_text: Clock skew scheduling is a cost-effective technique for enhancing synchronous digital VLSI systems. The technique simply involves adjusting the clock skew to meet signal path timing constraints in order to increase the clock frequency or timing yield. Traditionally, Gaussian distributions have been assumed for path delays under process variations. However, this assumption may be inappropriate due to the notable asymmetry of actual path delay distributions. In this paper, we propose the generalized extreme value (GEV) distribution as a potential alternative, along with a hybrid distribution approach that utilizes different distributions for different path delays to improve accuracy. We also analyze three parameter estimation methods: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), L-moments, and the method of moments (MoM) to evaluate the accuracy of the fit. Our experimental results show that the GEV distribution more accurately approximates path delays in benchmark circuits, achieving an average improvement of 40% and 30% in the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistic compared to the Gaussian and Lognormal distributions, respectively. In addition, Q-Q (Quantile-Quantile) and P-P (Probability-Probability) plots are employed to visually validate the goodness-of-fit for different distributions. For timing yield-driven CSS, the hybrid method achieves the highest performance, improving yield by an average of 6% over the Gaussian model and by 2% over the GEV-based model. These results demonstrate that the hybrid distribution approach effectively captures heterogeneous path behavior and provides robust yield optimization.

items.abstract_text: As transistor dimensions continue to scale down aggressively, the lateral overgrowth of source/drain (S/D) epitaxy has emerged as a critical limitation. When the spacing between transistors becomes narrow, uncontrolled lateral overgrowth can cause the merging of S/D regions in adjacent transistors, leading to fatal errors such as electrical shorts. The introduction of a fence structure effectively suppresses this overgrowth, thereby enabling cell size reduction and improved integration density. However, it also introduces complex changes in device characteristics, including increased contact and S/D resistance, as well as reduced parasitic capacitance. In this work, we systematically analyzed the impact of the fence structure from a Design-Technology Co-Optimization (DTCO) perspective. The DC performance of transistors was evaluated based on the linear mode on-state current (IDS,LIN), effective drive current (IEFF), and saturation mode on-state current (IDS,SAT). For transient response characterization, we investigated the propagation delay (high-to-low;tpHLand low-to-high propagation delay;tpLH) of CMOS inverters under two configurations—Fan-Out 0 (FO0) and Fan-Out 3 (FO3)—to assess both intrinsic device characteristics and circuit-level behavior. The results demonstrate that optimized fence implementation can achieve performance gains while simultaneously enhancing integration density, thereby providing significant design advantages in advanced semiconductor technologies.

items.title: Fully Automated Schematic and Layout Design of Millimeter-Wave CMOS Power Amplifiers Using Prior Knowledge-Guided Decomposition and Machine Learning-Assisted Optimization
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: The RF CMOS technology is preferably used in the development of mass-market millimeter-wave (mmWave) integrated circuits because of its cost-effectiveness and integration capabilities. However, conventional design methods, limited by fixed topologies, struggle to achieve optimal performance, power, and area (PPA) trade-offs. A fully automated method is proposed for rapid mmWave CMOS power amplifier (PA) design that uses prior knowledge-guided decomposition and machine learning-assisted optimization (MLAO). Following hybrid topology configuration through schematic simulation, the proposed approach decomposes the entire circuit into multiple optimizable subproblems using microwave network theory. Then, these subproblems are solved sequentially and iteratively. In particular, a multibranch MLAO algorithm is applied to on-chip transformers to enable broadband matching and high-fidelity impedance synthesis. Post-layout simulation results for five different PA design cases, spanning 17 to 41 GHz, demonstrate that the proposed method significantly accelerates the design process compared to conventional approaches while maintaining a high PPA.

items.abstract_text: As cryptographic hardware implementations become increasingly widespread, the security of their embedded cryptographic modules faces growing threats from side-channel analysis (SCA). Deep learning-based profiled side-channel analysis has been shown to effectively break masking countermeasures, which are designed to protect sensitive intermediate computations from SCA. However, these techniques typically rely on mask leakage, which severely limits their effectiveness when such leakage is unknown, obscured, or temporally distant, as the profiling model cannot effectively exploit it. In this work, we combine the principles of collision attacks and propose a mask-independent collision-based profiled approach named MICA. By reformulating key recovery as a collision detection problem, MICA can identify identical intermediate values within cryptographic computations from SCA leakage, even when the corresponding leakage characteristics differ due to implementation variations across processing units. Moreover, MICA can recover key differences without relying on mask leakage by exploiting repeated computations and potential mask reuse. Extensive experiments on various AES hardware implementations demonstrate that MICA consistently outperforms other theoretically sound profiled SCAs as well as state-of-the-art collision-based attacks.

items.abstract_text: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are widely used in sequence-based tasks such as speech recognition and sentiment analysis. However, the presence of gating units significantly increases computational overhead and memory usage, making LSTMs less suitable for resource-constrained edge devices and latency-sensitive applications. To address this, various model compression techniques, such as pruning and structured weight, have been explored to reduce memory access and computational demands. However, deploying these compressed models on conventional LSTM accelerators often suffer from low compute efficiency, limiting their practical applicability. This paper proposes a novel column-wise pruning method that adaptively adjusts the sparsity of gating matrices based on their sensitivity to model accuracy, thereby maximizing overall sparsity. To further reduce computational complexity, the sparse vectors processed using the delta network (DN) efficiently skips zero elements during matrix computations. Moreover, we introduce a highly optimized column-wise hardware architecture tailored for efficient LSTM inference. Our accelerator is implemented on an AMD Zynq 7000 XC7Z100 FPGA and evaluated using the TIMIT dataset. Experimental results demonstrate an 80.5× model compression rate without accuracy loss, and 24.8 Top/s of effective throughput. Compared to state-of-the-art LSTM accelerators, our design achieves 2.6× ∼ 27× speedup and 2.3× ∼ 25× improvement in energy efficiency.

items.abstract_text: Advanced fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) has become a key enabler for high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence (AI) systems, offering high-density and heterogeneous integration of chips. As the interconnect density of signal nets in redistribution layers (RDLs) continues to increase, ensuring reliability and manufacturability becomes increasingly challenging. To ensure reliable power delivery, signal nets are required to minimize their wire usage within fan-in regions to reserve routing space for power delivery networks (PDNs). Meanwhile, specific fan-out routing patterns in keep-out-zones (KOZs) and chip boundaries are essential for improving manufacturing yield. While these advanced design rules improve packaging reliability and manufacturability, they also increase routing difficulty due to constrained fan-out space and specific fan-out routing patterns in the KOZs and chip boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose a redistribution layer routing method for fan-out wafer-level packaging considering multiple advanced design rules that offers improved reliability and manufacturability by implementing five major techniques: 1) A KOZ-aware channel generation technique and a well-designed directed 2D global routing graph are proposed to analyze routing resources of limited fan-out regions and avoid the violations in KOZs and chip boundaries. 2) A bipartite matching algorithm is employed for global net-to-bump assignment, minimizing wirelength while avoiding locally suboptimal solutions. 3) We generate multiple candidate 2D global routing paths using a K-shortest path algorithm, enabling each net to explore candidate wirelength-minimized and congestion-avoiding routing paths. 4) We formulate the path selection problem as an integer linear programming (ILP) model to globally assign minimum-length routing paths while satisfying routing capacity constraints. 5) We propose a 3D routing framework to perform intra-channel routing using an octagonal-tile-based 3D global routing and a geometry-based detailed routing to minimize the final routing wirelength while avoiding conflicts and satisfying spacing constraints. The experimental results show that our algorithm achieves 100% routability without violations in KOZs or chip boundaries, while reducing fan-in usage by 25.13× and 14.31× on average compared with two leading RDL routers.

items.title: Softm e x : Lightweight Softmax Compute Engines Based on Exponentiation Units
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: This paper presents efficient compute engines for the softmax function, collectively named Softmex. In Softmex, the logarithm of the function’s denominator is computed incrementally in a numerically stable manner based on the log-sum-exp trick, without normalization which involves searching for the maximum input and subtracting it. Furthermore, the logarithm is computed efficiently based on exponentiation. The proposed engines are designed primarily with exponentiation units; no normalizing units, nor those required to compute logarithm and reciprocal. Implementation results in a 45nm CMOS technology show that one of the proposed engines achieves 4.4 times higher area efficiency than the previous state-of-the-art work while maintaining the inference quality in practical transformer-based models.

items.abstract_text: Timing optimization during global placement is critical for achieving optimal circuit performance and remains a key challenge in modern Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) design. As FPGA designs scale and heterogeneous resources increase, dense interconnects introduce significant resistive and capacitive effects, making timing closure increasingly difficult. Existing methods face challenges in constructing accurate timing models due to multi-factor nonlinear constraints as well as load and crosstalk coupling effects arising in multi-pin driving scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose TD-Placer, a critical path aware, timing-driven global placement framework. It leverages graph-based representations to capture global net interactions and employs a nonlinear model to integrate diverse timing-related features for precise delay prediction, thereby improving the overall placement quality for FPGAs. TD-Placer adopts a quadratic placement objective that minimizes wirelength while incorporating a timing term constructed by a lightweight algorithm, enabling efficient and high-quality timing optimization. Regarding net-level timing contention, it also employs a finer-grained weighting scheme to facilitate smooth reduction of the Critical Path Delay (CPD). Extensive experiments were carried out on seven real-world open-source FPGA projects with LUT counts ranging from 60K to 400K. The results demonstrate that TD-Placer achieves an average ∼10% improvement in Worst Negative Slack (WNS) and a ∼5% reduction in CPD compared to the state-of-the-art method, with an average CPD comparable (×1.01) to the commercial AMD Vivado across five versions (2020.2–2024.2). Its code and dataset are publicly available1.

items.title: A Universal and Lightweight Automated Design Framework for Multiband Power Amplifiers
items.journal: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.venue_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
items.summary: In power amplifier (PA) design, the repeated trial-and-error process and time-consuming electromagnetic (EM) simulation are major obstacles to achieving efficient design. In this study, based on a small microstrip line dataset, a lightweight deep neural network (DNN) is trained to accurately predict the S-parameters of layout-level matching networks (MNs). Leveraging the DNN’s high-speed prediction capabilities and an ordinary particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm, the entire optimization process is completed without the involvement of EM simulation software, enabling highly efficient automated design of PAs. This method is applied to the automated synthesis of narrowband, tri-band, and broadband PAs, demonstrating high flexibility. Among these, the broadband PA (a 0.5-5 GHz GaN PA) is fabricated for validation. Measurement results show that within the operating frequency range, the output power reaches 39-42.2 dBm, and the drain efficiency (DE) ranges from 47.2% to 74.6%, with an average of 56.5%.

items.abstract_text: Deep learning-based computer vision models involve extensive matrix multiplications, leading to high computational costs. Logarithmic quantization reduces resource consumption by replacing multiplications with shift operations. However, the recent Selective Two-word Log Quantization (STLQ) introduces hardware design challenges. It introduces unstructured sparsity which lowers hardware utilization and requires separate scaling factors which increase buffer demands. Additionally, we observe that many multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in log-quantized matrix multiplications are redundant, offering an opportunity to improve accelerator design. In this work, we propose two key techniques to address the challenges and opportunities in designing a resource-efficient log-quantized matrix multiplication accelerator. First, Hardware-friendly Selective Two-word Log Quantization (HSTLQ) imposes a regular sparsity pattern during the second round quantization and safely eliminates the second word scaling factors. Second, Log-similar Pattern Skipping (LPS) precomputes similar MAC patterns and reuses the precomputed results, thereby eliminating redundant operations. In the end, by integrating HSTLQ and LPS with novel circuit design, we propose an hardware accelerator for log-quantized General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM), and it achieves high energy and area efficiency of 9.53 TOPS/W and 1135.3 GOPS/mm2, making it an attractive solution for edge devices.

items.abstract_text: The ability to adapt to changing environments is crucial for the autonomous navigation systems of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). However, existing navigation systems adopt fixed execution configurations without considering environmental dynamics based on available computing resources, e.g., with a high execution frequency and task workload. This static approach causes rigid flight strategies and excessive computations, ultimately degrading flight performance or even leading to failures in UAVs. Despite the necessity for an adaptive system, dynamically adjusting workloads remains challenging, due to difficulties in quantifying environmental complexity and modeling the relationship between environment and system configuration. Aiming at adapting to dynamic environments, this paper proposes E-Navi, an environmental-adaptive navigation system for UAVs that dynamically adjusts task executions on the CPUs in response to environmental changes based on available computational resources. Specifically, the perception-planning pipeline of UAVs navigation system is redesigned through dynamic adaptation of mapping resolution and execution frequency, driven by the quantitative environmental complexity evaluations. In addition, E-Navi supports flexible deployment across hardware platforms with varying levels of computing capability. Extensive Hardware-In-the-Loop and real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed system significantly outperforms the baseline method across various hardware platforms, achieving up to 53.9% navigation task workload reduction, up to 63.8% flight time savings, and delivering more stable velocity control.

This trend underscores the need for automated and effective debugging solutions. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong analytical capabilities in program understanding and debugging, offering a novel perspective for bug localization in Register Transfer Level (RTL) designs. In this paper, we propose LocFree, a LLM-based framework for bug localization in RTL designs using hierarchical reasoning. LocFree comprises two main phases: the prompt generation phase and the bug localization phase. In the prompt generation phase, LocFree extracts four critical features from the Verilog code and its corresponding testbench: metadata feature, semantic structure feature, timing pattern feature, and testbench feature. It then employs these features in a hierarchical reasoning process to generates an optimized prompt that guides the LLM toward precise bug localization. In the bug localization phase, LocFree leverages the optimized prompt in conjunction with the LLM to identify the faults in the RTL designs. Experimental evaluation on 26 Verilog designs containing 397 bugs demonstrates that LocFree significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, our approach successfully localizes 76.8%, 82.5%, and 87.3% of bugs within the Top-1, Top-3, and Top-5 ranks, respectively—substantially exceeding the performance of existing bug localization methods.

items.abstract_text: As circuit feature sizes continue to scale down in advanced technology nodes, layout printability has become increasingly challenging, making lithographic hotspot detection an ever more difficult task in computer-aided design (CAD) flows. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a key enabler in identifying lithographic hotspots, with numerous studies reporting encouraging results. However, neural networks can become prone to bias and overfitting, especially when trained on limited data—a common crux in the CAD domain. A generalizable deep learning (DL)-based hotspot detector should learn the genuine lithography principle and ensure consistent accuracy across layouts from various designs at the same technology node, regardless of their varying design styles. However, we find that existing convolutional neural network (CNN)-based hotspot detectors fail to generalize to different circuit layouts other than the design for which they were trained. To this end, we propose a few-shot learning-based framework for generalizable CNN-based hotspot detection. We propose a meta-learning scheme that asynchronously updates the CNN feature extraction and classification components to obtain a meta-initialized model that can quickly adapt to new designs using as few as one training layout clip. Specifically, following a label-free layout feature-based clustering, we develop an accuracy estimation method that selects the most accurate meta-initial model for new designs. We additionally introduce a geometry-based sampling strategy that selects representative layout clips for few-shot adaptation, thereby enhancing generalization stability. Experimental results on the ICCAD 2012 and 2019 datasets demonstrate that our framework offers superior generalization capabilities compared to prior art on unseen new designs. This paper extends our previous work [1].

Concurrently, the rapid iteration of robotic deployment scenarios demands an agile and scalable hardware development methodology.
